META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 2.7 (8 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Essential Mathematics
UNIT.content:
• Volume and capacity of cones: deriving and applying the formula V = ⅓πr²h; relating to the volume of a cylinder of equal base and height
• Volume and capacity of pyramids (square and rectangular base): deriving and applying V = ⅓ × base area × height
• Volume and capacity of frustums of cones: applying V = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²) using dimensions of the original cone and the removed top cone
• Volume and capacity of frustums of pyramids: applying V = ⅓h(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)) for square and rectangular bases
• Relationship between volume units and capacity units (cm³ ↔ mL, m³ ↔ L; 1 L = 1 000 cm³)
• Reading and interpreting measurements of real containers (buckets, grain stores, water tanks, cooking pots) shaped as cones, pyramids and frustums
• Selecting and applying appropriate formulae to solve real-life volume and capacity problems
• Project: making and measuring model containers shaped as frustums, pyramids and cones from locally available materials
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) determine the volume and capacity of cones and pyramids,
b) compute volume and capacity of a frustum of a cone,
c) calculate the volume and capacity of a frustum of a pyramid,
d) apply volume and capacity in real-life situations,
e) appreciate volumes and capacities in real life situations.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: the learner acquires open-mindedness and creativity skills when discussing with peers and working out the volume and capacity of containers shaped as cones, pyramids and frustums; learners must choose and justify the correct formula for each shape encountered.
• Creativity and Imagination: the learner develops connection and networking skills when deriving the volume of frustums by subtracting a smaller cone or pyramid from a larger one, and when constructing physical models of these solids from locally available materials such as cardboard, old packaging and clay.
UNIT.values:
• Unity: the learner displays tolerance of different opinions while working with peers when constructing models of frustums as learning resources, sharing materials equitably and dividing tasks fairly within the group.
• Respect: the learner listens to others' opinions while discussing appropriate formulae for working out volume and capacity of containers, and acknowledges contributions of group members during presentations.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking Questions and Defining Problems: learners pose questions about why different containers (buckets, grain stores, water tanks) hold different amounts even when they look similar in height, initiating the mathematical investigation of volume and capacity.
• Developing and Using Models: learners build physical models of cones, pyramids and frustums to visualise the relationship between a frustum and its parent solid, then use mathematical formulae as abstract models to predict capacity.
• Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking: learners select and apply the appropriate volume formula, substitute measured dimensions, and convert between volume units (cm³, m³) and capacity units (mL, L) to solve real-life container problems.
• Constructing Explanations: learners explain why V(frustum) = V(large cone) − V(small cone) by referencing their physical models and measurements, justifying each step of their working.
UNIT.pcis:
• Environment and Technology: the learner uses appropriate containers from the local environment — such as plastic buckets used for carrying water from the borehole, metal grain-storage bins common in Rift Valley farms, and cooking pots used for ugali — to work out the capacity of cones, pyramids and their frustums, promoting environmental awareness and resourcefulness.
• Education for Sustainable Development: by calculating the capacity of water-harvesting tanks and grain-storage structures shaped as frustums, learners connect mathematics to sustainable food and water management practices relevant to Kenyan farming communities.
UNIT.careers:
• Civil and Structural Engineering: calculating volumes of conical and pyramidal roof structures, water tanks and grain silos used in construction projects across Kenya.
• Architecture and Interior Design: determining capacity of decorative containers, lamp shades and furniture components with frustum or pyramidal shapes.
• Agriculture and Food Science: estimating grain storage capacity of pyramidal or frustum-shaped stores; calculating volumes of conical heaps of maize or beans at market stalls in Wakulima Market, Nairobi.
• Manufacturing and Packaging: designing and sizing packaging (e.g., paper funnels, ice-cream cones, juice cartons) for the food and beverage industry in Kenyan factories.
• Hospitality and Catering: working out capacities of cooking vessels and serving containers in hotels and restaurants along the Kenyan coast and urban centres such as Kisumu and Mombasa.
• Water Resources Management: computing the volume of water stored in conical or frustum-shaped tanks for community water projects in arid and semi-arid areas of Kenya.
UNIT.focus: This unit develops learners' ability to calculate the volume and capacity of cones, pyramids and their frustums, rooting every concept in Kenyan everyday objects such as water-carrying buckets, grain-storage bins and cooking pots. Learners move from establishing the cone–cylinder relationship through hands-on measurement of real containers to applying and justifying formulae for frustums of both cones and pyramids. The unit culminates in a project in which learners design, build and document model containers, connecting geometry to sustainable resource management in the Kenyan context.
UNIT.phenomenon: A group of farmers in Kericho have three different containers they use to store harvested tea leaves before collection: a tall cylindrical drum, a conical heap-cover made from woven sisal, and a metal bucket (frustum of a cone) used for carrying leaves to the weighing station. All three containers have roughly the same height and the same opening diameter, yet when filled with water the cylindrical drum holds exactly three times as much water as the conical cover, and the metal bucket holds noticeably more water than the cone but less than the cylinder. Learners observe these three containers side by side, filled with water, and are puzzled: why do shapes that look so similar in size hold such dramatically different amounts? This anchoring phenomenon drives the entire unit — learners must unpack the mathematical relationship between a cone and a cylinder, then extend that reasoning to pyramids and frustums, to explain and predict the capacities of the containers used every day by Kenyan tea farmers.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• A mandazi vendor in Mombasa uses a conical paper bag and a frustum-shaped plastic cup to pack mandazi for customers; the vendor claims both hold the same number of mandazi, but customers dispute this — learners investigate whether the volumes are truly equal given the same slant height.
• A water-harvesting project near Lake Turkana installs frustum-shaped underground cisterns; community members want to know how many 20-litre jerricans can be filled from a cistern of given top diameter, bottom diameter and depth — learners calculate the capacity and convert to jerricans.
• A Nairobi school's mathematics club builds a square pyramidal display stand for their science fair; the teacher asks them to fill it with sand to find its volume experimentally, then compare the result to the formula — learners reconcile measured and calculated values.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: Why do the tea farmers' containers — a cone, a cylinder and a bucket — look nearly the same size but hold such different amounts of water, and how can we use mathematics to design a frustum-shaped container that holds exactly the capacity we need?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTION:
1. Why is the knowledge of volume and capacity useful?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1 — Predict & Anchor Phenomenon: Learners examine the three Kericho tea-farmer containers (or physical models/images thereof). They predict which holds the most water, record estimates, and articulate what they wonder. The driving question is introduced and posted on the Driving Question Board. Learners review the relationship between volume units (cm³, m³) and capacity units (mL, L) as prerequisite knowledge.

Lesson 2 — Cone vs. Cylinder (Observe & Explain): Using a cone and cylinder of identical base radius and height (models or demonstration containers), learners fill the cone with water and pour it into the cylinder three times to observe that V(cylinder) = 3 × V(cone). They derive the cone volume formula V = ⅓πr²h, apply it to the Kericho conical cover, and calculate its capacity in litres. Learners update the DQB with new understanding.

Lesson 3 — Volume of Pyramids (Observe & Explain): Learners use models of a square-based pyramid and a cuboid of equal base and height to establish V(pyramid) = ⅓ × base area × height. They apply the formula to pyramidal grain-store models, computing volumes and converting to capacity. They compare results with their Lesson 1 predictions and refine the DQB.

Lesson 4 — Introducing Frustums of Cones (Explain & Model Building): Learners measure a real frustum-shaped bucket (top radius R, bottom radius r, height h) and the dimensions of the full cone from which it could be cut. They derive V(frustum of cone) = V(large cone) − V(small cone) = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²) step by step. They calculate the bucket's capacity and compare it to the cylindrical drum, resolving the anchoring phenomenon.

Lesson 5 — Volume of Frustums of Pyramids (Explain & Model Building): Learners extend the frustum concept to square and rectangular pyramidal frustums using V = ⅓h(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)). They apply the formula to a pyramidal grain-storage bin model, compute capacity in litres and kilograms of maize (using density), and update their cumulative models on the DQB.

Lesson 6 — Problem Solving with Real Containers (Apply & DQB Update): Learners work in groups on a set of Kenyan-context word problems: sizing a conical water tank for a homestead in Turkana, calculating the capacity of a frustum-shaped cooking pot used in a githeri recipe for 100 people, and determining how many frustum-shaped cups fill a cylindrical storage drum. Groups present solutions and justify formula choices; the DQB is updated with consolidated understanding.

Lesson 7 — Project: Model Making & Measurement: Learners design and construct model containers shaped as a frustum of a cone, a frustum of a pyramid and a cone using locally available materials (cardboard from cereal boxes, old packaging). They measure dimensions, calculate theoretical volumes and capacities, then fill models with water or sand to verify experimentally. Discrepancies between theoretical and measured values are discussed. Photographs and video clips are taken for documentation.

Lesson 8 — Model Building Culmination & Assessment: Groups present their project models, share calculated and measured capacities, and explain sources of error. The class revisits the anchoring phenomenon — the Kericho farmers' containers — and constructs a final annotated diagram showing the volume relationships between cone, cylinder, pyramid and frustum. A written class activity assesses all five specific learning outcomes. The DQB is completed and learners articulate what they now know versus what they predicted in Lesson 1.

LESSONS.title: The Kericho Container Puzzle: Anchoring the Phenomenon & Launching the Driving Question

slo.purpose: To anchor learners in the phenomenon of three Kericho tea-farmer containers (cylinder, cone, frustum) that look the same size yet hold dramatically different amounts of water, and to activate prerequisite knowledge of volume and capacity units.
slo.knowledge: Learners recall and articulate the relationship between volume units (cm³, m³) and capacity units (mL, L); learners identify the names and key features (height, base radius, slant) of a cylinder, cone, and frustum (bucket) as seen in the Kericho tea-farming context.
slo.skills: Learners make and record quantitative predictions; learners estimate and compare capacities of the three containers; learners formulate questions about the phenomenon and post them on the Driving Question Board.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that mathematics embedded in everyday Kenyan farm tools can reveal surprising and useful truths; learners demonstrate curiosity, honesty in recording predictions, and respect for peers' differing estimates.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is the knowledge of volume and capacity useful?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the opening lesson of the unit. Learners encounter the anchoring phenomenon — three containers used by Kericho tea farmers that appear similar in size but hold strikingly different volumes of water. By predicting, observing side-by-side images or physical models, and articulating their wonderings, learners generate the intellectual need that will drive the entire unit. The Driving Question Board is opened and the unit's driving question is posted. Prerequisite knowledge of cm³/m³ ↔ mL/L conversions is reviewed so learners have the language to quantify their predictions in subsequent lessons.
slo.safetyNotes: If physical containers with water are used, place a plastic sheet or basin under the demonstration area to prevent slipping on wet floors. Learners handle models carefully; no sharp cutting tools are used in this lesson.

LESSONS.overview: Learners are introduced to the unit's anchoring phenomenon: three containers used by Kericho tea farmers — a tall cylindrical drum, a conical sisal heap-cover, and a metal frustum-shaped bucket — that have nearly the same height and opening diameter yet hold dramatically different amounts of water. Working individually first, then in pairs, learners study images or physical models, predict which container holds the most and least water, record numerical estimates in litres, and share their reasoning. The class articulates what surprises them and what they wonder, generating questions that are posted on the newly opened Driving Question Board. The teacher then facilitates a brief prerequisite review connecting cm³ to mL and m³ to L, equipping learners with the unit language they will need throughout. The lesson closes with the formal posting of the unit Driving Question.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner receives a printed A5 observation sheet showing three side-by-side labelled diagrams of the Kericho tea-farmer containers: Container A (cylinder), Container B (cone, apex down), and Container C (frustum/bucket). Dimensions shown: all three have a height of approximately 30 cm and a top opening diameter of approximately 20 cm. Learners study the diagrams silently for 2 minutes, then individually write responses to three prompts on their sheet: (1) Rank the containers from most to least water held — write your ranking and explain your reasoning in one sentence. (2) Estimate in litres how much water each container holds when filled to the brim. (3) Write one thing you notice and one thing you wonder about these containers. Learners then share their ranking and one estimate with a partner using a Think-Pair-Share, with each partner taking 30 seconds to explain their reasoning before hearing the other's view.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute observation sheets face-down. Say: 'Before we do any mathematics today, I want you to trust your eyes and your instincts — just like a tea farmer in Kericho would when choosing the right container for the job.' Flip sheets over on count of three. Allow 2 minutes of silent individual thinking — circulate and observe without commenting. After 2 minutes say: 'Now write your ranking — most to least — and your estimates in litres. You have 90 seconds.' After writing, say: 'Turn to your partner. Partner A, share your ranking and your reason — you have 30 seconds. Then Partner B responds.' After both share, cold-call 4 pairs (choose 1 pair who ranked C > A > B, 1 pair who ranked A > C > B, and 2 pairs with other rankings) using: 'Tell the class your ranking and the single most important reason behind it.' After each response, ask the class: 'Does anyone have a different reason for the same ranking?' Wait 10 seconds before calling on a volunteer. Record all three distinct rankings on the board in a simple tally. Do NOT confirm or deny any prediction — say: 'All of these rankings are on the board. By the end of this unit, every one of you will be able to prove which ranking is correct using mathematics.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share with ranked prediction: Learners first commit to a personal prediction in writing (individual accountability), then encounter a peer's potentially different view (cognitive conflict), which surfaces the phenomenon's puzzle before any instruction occurs. Recording all rankings publicly normalises uncertainty and establishes that the phenomenon is genuinely surprising.
framework.formativeAssessment: Teacher scans observation sheets during the silent phase to check: (a) all learners have attempted a ranking — redirect any blank sheets with 'Just write what your eyes tell you, there is no wrong answer yet'; (b) estimates are expressed as numbers with a unit — if a learner writes only 'big' or 'medium', prompt: 'Can you give me a number in litres or millilitres?' Cold-call responses reveal whether learners are reasoning from height alone, from the visual width, or from a vague sense of shape — this diagnostic informs which misconceptions to address in later lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher projects (or displays on printed A3 posters) a sequence of three photographs or diagrams taken from a Kericho tea farm: (i) the cylindrical drum alone, filled to the brim with water coloured with blue food dye; (ii) the conical sisal cover, filled to the brim — the same blue water is poured in and the level is visibly lower than expected; (iii) the frustum metal bucket, filled to the brim — water level is between the cone and the cylinder. A fourth image shows all three containers side by side, each filled to the brim, with measuring jugs placed next to each showing the actual capacities: A (cylinder) ≈ 9.4 L, B (cone) ≈ 3.1 L, C (frustum/bucket) ≈ 6.5 L. Learners record the actual capacities on their observation sheet, note whether their ranking was correct, and update their 'I wonder' statement based on what they now see. In groups of three, learners discuss: 'The cylinder holds almost exactly three times as much as the cone. What is it about the shape of the cone that could explain this?' Groups have 3 minutes to discuss and write a group hypothesis in one sentence.
framework.teacherMoves: Display images one at a time. Before revealing the fourth image say: 'I am about to show you the actual measured capacities. Before I do — look at your estimate. On your sheet, circle it.' Reveal the fourth image. Allow 30 seconds of silent reaction. Then say: 'Update your observation sheet — write the actual values and put a tick or cross next to your ranking.' Give 1 minute. Then say: 'In your groups of three, discuss this question' — write on board: 'The cylinder holds EXACTLY three times as much as the cone. What is it about the shape that makes this happen?' Allow 3 minutes of group discussion. Circulate: listen for groups who mention 'the cone gets narrower', 'less space inside', or 'the cone is pointy at the bottom'. After 3 minutes, cold-call 3 groups to share their hypothesis sentence. After each, say: 'Interesting — hold that idea. We will test it mathematically in Lessons 2 and 3.' Do NOT resolve the question yet. Say: 'What you have just observed is the puzzle at the heart of this entire unit. Kericho tea farmers deal with this every single harvest.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discrepant-event observation: The gap between learners' predictions and the actual capacities (especially the striking 3:1 cylinder-to-cone ratio) creates productive cognitive dissonance. This is the engine of inquiry — learners now have a genuine need to know why. The group hypothesis step moves learners from passive surprise to active preliminary explanation, practising the science and engineering practice of constructing explanations from evidence.
framework.formativeAssessment: Listen to group hypothesis sentences. Observable indicators of understanding: (a) groups that connect the cone's narrowing shape to less volume are ready for formal derivation (Lesson 2); (b) groups that only say 'the cone is smaller' without referencing shape change need the cylinder-cone comparison demonstration in Lesson 2 to be more hands-on; (c) groups that are fixated solely on the opening diameter rather than the 3D interior shape will benefit from the net-building activity. Record group names against these three categories in your register margin for differentiation planning.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher facilitates a whole-class prerequisite knowledge review: the relationship between volume units and capacity units. Learners receive a mini reference card (or copy into their notebooks): 1 cm³ = 1 mL; 1 000 cm³ = 1 L; 1 m³ = 1 000 L. Using the actual capacity of the cylindrical drum (≈ 9.4 L), learners individually convert: (a) 9.4 L → mL; (b) 9.4 L → cm³; (c) 3.1 L (cone) → cm³. They then compare: 'If Container A holds 9 400 cm³ and Container B holds 3 100 cm³, what is the ratio A : B in simplest form?' Learners write this on their sheet. A volunteer comes to the board to show the working. The class checks. The teacher then poses: 'So if we know the volume formula for the cylinder, could we use this ratio to find the formula for the cone?' Learners write this as a question on their sheet — it is the bridge to Lesson 2.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Before we can solve the Kericho farmers' puzzle mathematically, we need to make sure we all speak the same language of measurement. Let me show you the reference card.' Display or dictate the three conversion facts. Say: 'Using the actual capacities we observed, I want you to work these three conversions alone — silent work, 2 minutes.' After 2 minutes: 'Now the ratio — simplest form — 30 more seconds.' Cold-call one learner for (a), a different learner for (b), a third for (c), and a fourth for the ratio. For each, ask: 'Can someone tell me if they agree or disagree with that answer — and why?' Wait 10 seconds before accepting a response. After confirming 3 000 : 1 000 → 3 : 1, say: 'This ratio — 3 to 1 — is not a coincidence. It is a mathematical law. Your job over the next few lessons is to discover where that law comes from and how to use it.' Write on the board in a box: 'Cylinder volume : Cone volume = 3 : 1 (same base, same height) — WHY?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Anchored prerequisite review: Rather than reviewing unit conversions in isolation, the teacher uses the actual data from the phenomenon as the numbers for the conversion exercises. This anchors prerequisite knowledge directly to the driving question context, ensuring learners see cm³ and L not as abstract units but as the language for describing the Kericho containers. The ratio calculation plants the seed of the core algebraic relationship before formal derivation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Cold-call responses to the three conversions reveal: (a) learners who correctly convert all three are prerequisite-ready; (b) learners who confuse cm³ with cm or forget the factor of 1 000 need a brief individual follow-up — teacher writes the conversion ladder on a sticky note for those learners to keep in their notebook; (c) if more than 6 learners cannot state the simplest ratio, pause and reteach the conversion bridge using: 'How many mL are in 1 L? Good. So how many cm³ are in 9 400 mL?' before proceeding.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner writes two questions on separate sticky notes (or torn pieces of paper if sticky notes are unavailable): one question about why the containers hold different amounts, and one question about how the shape affects the volume. Learners post their sticky notes on the class Driving Question Board — a large sheet of manila paper divided into three columns: 'WHAT I NOTICE', 'WHAT I WONDER', 'WHAT I NEED TO LEARN'. The teacher reads aloud five representative questions and, with the class, sorts them into the three columns. The teacher then formally posts the unit Driving Question in large print at the top of the board: 'Why do the tea farmers' containers — a cone, a cylinder and a bucket — look nearly the same size but hold such different amounts of water, and how can we use mathematics to design a frustum-shaped container that holds exactly the capacity we need?' The class reads the driving question aloud together once. Learners copy it into their notebooks and underline or circle any words they are unsure about.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute two sticky notes (or paper squares) per learner. Say: 'On your first note, write a question that begins with WHY — something about these containers that you genuinely do not yet understand. On your second note, write a question that begins with HOW — something you would need to learn to design a better container for the Kericho farmers.' Allow 2 minutes of silent writing. Say: 'Come and post your notes — WHY questions on the left, HOW questions on the right. If you are not sure which column, post it in the middle.' Allow 2 minutes for posting. Read five questions aloud — choose ones that represent the range: one very specific ('Why is it exactly 3 times?'), one broad ('How do you calculate the volume of a weird shape?'), one applied ('How do farmers know which container to buy?'). After reading each, say: 'Which column do we think this belongs in?' Take a quick show of hands. After sorting, say: 'Every one of your questions is valid. Over the next lessons, we will answer each of them — and you will track your own growing understanding right here on this board.' Formally post and read the unit Driving Question. Say: 'This board will grow every lesson. By the last lesson of this unit, every sticky note on it will have an answer — an answer you worked out yourself.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Public Question Mapping: The DQB makes learner thinking visible and collective. By sorting questions into NOTICE / WONDER / NEED TO LEARN, learners practise distinguishing observations from inferences and identifying knowledge gaps — core practices of mathematical inquiry. The board also serves as a living formative assessment tool: the teacher can read it after class to plan the sequence of lessons 2–7.
framework.formativeAssessment: Scan sticky notes for question quality: (a) questions that name specific shapes ('Why does the cone get so much smaller?') show learners are attending to geometry — these learners are ready for formula derivation; (b) questions that are purely procedural ('What is the formula?') indicate learners need more phenomenon engagement — revisit the images at the start of Lesson 2; (c) absence of any HOW questions from a learner suggests they may not yet see mathematics as a design tool — check in with those learners during Lesson 2's group work.

framework.learnerExperience: As a closing activity, learners individually draw a first-draft annotated sketch of the three Kericho containers in their notebooks — a cylinder, a cone (apex down), and a frustum (bucket shape). They label: height, top diameter, and any other dimension they think might matter. Beneath the sketch they write one sentence that is their current best explanation for why the containers hold different amounts. This is their Initial Model — it will be revised in every subsequent lesson. Learners fold the page and write 'INITIAL MODEL — Lesson 1' on the outside so it can be found easily for future revision.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'To close today, I want you to draw and label the three containers from memory — cylinder, cone, bucket — and write your current best explanation for the capacity difference. This is not a test — it is a snapshot of your thinking today, and you will improve it every lesson.' Allow 4 minutes of quiet drawing and writing. Circulate and read sentences without correcting — simply note them. After 4 minutes: 'Fold the page, write INITIAL MODEL — Lesson 1 on the outside, and leave it in your notebook. Next lesson, you will open it and see how your thinking has changed.' Close the lesson by pointing to the Driving Question Board: 'The Kericho farmers need a better container. You are the mathematicians who are going to design it. See you next lesson.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Initial Model Snapshot: Drawing a labelled model before instruction forces learners to externalise their mental model of the containers and their current causal reasoning. Because this model will be physically revisited and revised in each lesson, it creates a tangible record of conceptual growth — a hallmark of model-based learning and a powerful motivator for learners who can see their own progress.
framework.formativeAssessment: Review initial model sentences after class. Categorise: (a) causal language ('The cone holds less because it narrows to a point so there is less space') — strong starting point; (b) comparative language only ('The cylinder is bigger than the cone') — learner is observing but not yet explaining; (c) no dimensional reasoning at all — learner will need additional scaffolding in Lesson 2 with a physical cone and cylinder. Use this to set the starting groups for Lesson 2's hands-on measurement activity.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider the following: (1) How many learners predicted the correct ranking (A > C > B)? If fewer than one-third were correct, the phenomenon is sufficiently surprising — good. If most were correct, probe whether they already know the cone formula, as you may need to accelerate to Lesson 3 faster. (2) Were learners able to articulate WHY questions, or did their DQB notes only contain HOW questions? A board dominated by HOW suggests learners see this as a procedure unit — revisit the phenomenon image at the start of Lesson 2 and ask: 'What is it about the cone's shape — not its formula — that causes it to hold less?' (3) Review the initial model sentences: what is the modal level of explanation across the class? This tells you how much time to spend on the physical cylinder-cone water-pouring demonstration in Lesson 2. (4) Were any learners disengaged during the prediction phase? Consider assigning those learners the role of 'official recorder' on the DQB in Lesson 2 to increase buy-in. (5) Did the prerequisite review of cm³ ↔ L reveal significant gaps? If more than 8 learners struggled with the conversions, begin Lesson 2 with a 5-minute targeted review using the Kericho container data before moving to formula derivation.

LESSONS.title: Cone vs. Cylinder — Deriving the Cone Volume Formula

slo.purpose: To establish, through direct observation and guided reasoning, that the volume of a cone is exactly one-third the volume of a cylinder sharing the same base radius and height, and to apply the derived formula V = ⅓πr²h to calculate the capacity of the Kericho conical tea-cover.
slo.knowledge: Learners will know that: (a) a cone and a cylinder of equal base radius and height satisfy V(cylinder) = 3 × V(cone); (b) the volume formula for a cone is V = ⅓πr²h; (c) capacity in litres is obtained by converting cm³ using 1 litre = 1 000 cm³.
slo.skills: Learners will be able to: (a) measure the base radius and height of a cone and cylinder; (b) use repeated pouring to gather quantitative evidence of the 1:3 ratio; (c) derive and write the cone volume formula algebraically; (d) substitute given dimensions into V = ⅓πr²h and convert the result to litres; (e) update the class Driving Question Board with new evidence.
slo.attitudes: Learners will: appreciate that careful measurement and systematic observation lead to reliable mathematical generalisations; value the relevance of geometry to the daily work of Kenyan tea farmers; demonstrate patience, precision and collaborative respect during the pouring demonstration.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is the knowledge of volume and capacity useful?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1 learners recorded their initial predictions about why the three Kericho containers hold different amounts despite looking similar. Lesson 2 is the first major evidence-gathering lesson: learners directly observe the cone–cylinder pouring experiment, derive V = ⅓πr²h, and use it to calculate the actual capacity of the conical sisal cover. This gives them the first precise number to anchor the rest of the unit and deepens the puzzle — the cone holds only one-third as much as the cylinder, so why does the metal bucket (frustum) hold more than the cone but less than the cylinder?
slo.safetyNotes: Use plastic or metal containers for the pouring demonstration to avoid glass breakage. Wipe up any water spills immediately to prevent slipping. If food colouring is added to the water for visibility, remind learners it may stain clothing.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by revisiting their Lesson 1 predictions recorded on the Driving Question Board about the three Kericho tea-farmer containers. The teacher introduces a physical demonstration: a transparent plastic cylinder and a matching cone (identical base radius r and height h). Learners predict how many cones of water will fill the cylinder, then observe the repeated-pouring experiment three times. Using the known cylinder formula V = πr²h as an anchor, learners deduce that V(cone) = ⅓πr²h. They then apply the formula to the specific dimensions of the Kericho conical sisal cover (r = 21 cm, h = 42 cm), calculate its volume in cm³, convert to litres, and record the result as the first confirmed data point on the Driving Question Board. The lesson closes with a model-building update and targeted formative exit questions.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually write a prediction in their exercise books: 'How many full cones of water do you think it will take to completely fill the matching cylinder?' They then share predictions with a partner (Think-Pair-Share) and the class records a show-of-hands tally on the board (options: 1, 2, 3, 4, more than 4). Learners also sketch the cone and cylinder side by side, labelling what they already know: same opening diameter, same height — reinforcing the connection to the Kericho phenomenon.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the two physical containers (cone and cylinder, same r and h) prominently. Say: 'These represent the tall cylindrical drum and the conical sisal cover the Kericho farmers use. They have exactly the same opening width and the same height. Before we pour a single drop, I want your best mathematical guess — how many cones of water will fill the cylinder?' Allow 10 seconds of silent thinking (WAIT TIME). Cold-call 4 learners for their predictions and record each on the board. Then say: 'Hold that prediction. We are going to find out together right now.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Think-Pair-Share with class tally: activates prior knowledge of cylinder volume (V = πr²h from Junior School) and creates cognitive dissonance when the result surprises learners who predicted 1 or 2. The public tally makes predictions visible and personally invested.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: learner can correctly label r and h on both shapes in their sketch. Listen for whether learners spontaneously mention πr²h — this reveals recall of the cylinder formula, which will be needed in the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher (or a volunteer learner) fills the cone to the brim with water (coloured blue with food dye for visibility) and pours it into the cylinder. This is repeated a second and third time. Learners complete an observation table in their books with three columns: Pour Number | Water level in cylinder (estimate as fraction of height) | Running total (cones poured). After the third pour the cylinder is exactly full. Learners record the key observation: 3 cones = 1 cylinder. A short 3-minute silent reading extract (one paragraph) is then provided, describing how Kenyan agricultural extension officers at the Kericho Tea Development Authority use volume calculations to specify container sizes for tea-leaf collection — grounding the mathematics in a real professional context.
framework.teacherMoves: Before pouring, say: 'Watch the water level carefully after each pour. In your table, write a fraction — is it one-quarter full, one-half full, two-thirds full? Be precise.' Carry out Pour 1. WAIT 10 seconds after the water settles. Ask: 'What fraction of the cylinder is now filled? Turn to your neighbour — 10 seconds.' Cold-call 3 learners. Carry out Pour 2 and repeat questioning. Carry out Pour 3 — the cylinder is full. Say: 'What did we observe?' Cold-call 2 learners and require them to state it as a complete sentence: 'Three cones of water exactly fill one cylinder of the same base and height.' Distribute the short reading extract on the Tea Development Authority. After 3 minutes say: 'Underline one sentence that connects what we just saw to why a farmer or an extension officer would need to know this.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured observation table with fractional estimation: this forces quantitative attention at each stage rather than a single end-point observation, building the proportional reasoning needed to generalise the 1:3 ratio. The reading extract (Evidence from Text strategy) anchors the abstract observation in a professional Kenyan agricultural context, reinforcing the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: learner's observation table shows entries of approximately ⅓ full after Pour 1, ⅔ full after Pour 2, and completely full after Pour 3. Listen for learners who state the ratio as '3 cones = 1 cylinder' unprompted — they are ready for the algebraic derivation. Flag learners who write '2 cones' or express surprise — they need the derive step most.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work through a guided derivation in three steps written in their books: (Step 1) Write the cylinder formula: V(cylinder) = πr²h. (Step 2) Use the observation: V(cylinder) = 3 × V(cone). (Step 3) Therefore: V(cone) = πr²h ÷ 3 = ⅓πr²h. Learners then immediately apply the formula to the Kericho conical sisal cover: given r = 21 cm and height h = 42 cm, calculate (a) volume in cm³ and (b) capacity in litres. They compare this figure to the cylindrical drum (same r = 21 cm, h = 42 cm) calculated in a worked example on the board, and record the ratio 1:3 numerically using actual values. Learners also write one sentence explaining to a Kericho farmer why the cone-shaped cover cannot be used to store the same amount of water as the cylindrical drum even though both containers 'look the same size'.
framework.teacherMoves: Write on the board: 'We know V(cylinder) = πr²h. We just saw V(cylinder) = 3 × V(cone). So V(cone) = ?' WAIT 15 seconds of silent working time. Cold-call 2 learners to complete the algebra on the board. Confirm the formula: V = ⅓πr²h. Then say: 'Now let us use this formula for the actual Kericho conical sisal cover. I'll give you the measurements: radius 21 cm, height 42 cm. Work it out — you have 5 minutes.' Circulate and look at 6 books. After 5 minutes, cold-call one learner to write their working on the board. Guide the class to check: V = ⅓ × π × 21² × 42 = ⅓ × π × 441 × 42 ≈ ⅓ × 58 120 ≈ 19 373 cm³ ≈ 19.4 litres. Ask: 'So the conical cover holds about how many litres?' Cold-call 3 learners. Then say: 'Write one sentence — pretend you are explaining this to a Kericho tea farmer who has never studied mathematics. Why does the cone hold less?' WAIT 10 seconds, then pair-share before cold-calling 2 learners to read their sentences aloud.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Guided algebraic derivation (Claim-Evidence-Reasoning): learners construct the formula themselves using the observation as evidence rather than receiving it as a given rule. This strategy builds understanding of why the formula has a factor of ⅓, not just what the formula is. The farmer-explanation sentence forces learners to translate formal mathematics into contextual meaning, deepening conceptual ownership.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: learner's written derivation shows all three steps with correct algebraic manipulation. Correct numerical answer: V ≈ 19 373 cm³ ≈ 19.4 litres. Listen for learners who write 'V = πr²h ÷ 3' without connecting it to the observation — prompt them: 'What did the pouring tell us first?' Flag learners who forget to divide by 3 or use diameter instead of radius — these are the two most common errors at this stage.

framework.learnerExperience: The class DQB (a large chart on the wall) has three columns: What we observed | What we now know | What we still wonder. Each learner writes two sticky notes: one for 'What we now know' (e.g. 'The conical cover holds about 19.4 litres — exactly ⅓ of the cylinder') and one for 'What we still wonder' (e.g. 'The metal bucket holds more than the cone — is there a formula for that shape too?'). Sticky notes are placed on the DQB. The teacher reads two or three aloud and connects them explicitly to the driving question about the frustum-shaped bucket.
framework.teacherMoves: Point to the original driving question displayed above the DQB: 'Why do the three Kericho containers look nearly the same size but hold such different amounts?' Say: 'We have just answered part of this question for the cone. Write your two sticky notes — one for what you now know for certain, and one question you still have. You have 3 minutes.' After placing notes, read 2 from 'What we now know' and 2 from 'What we still wonder' aloud. Say: 'Notice that many of you are asking about the metal bucket — that shape between the cone and the cylinder. That is exactly where we are going next. Keep that question burning.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board update (public knowledge-tracking): making individual understanding visible to the whole class builds collective sense of progress, validates students' remaining confusion as productive, and creates explicit anticipation for the frustum lessons. The act of writing forces metacognitive reflection on what changed during this lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: learner's 'What we now know' sticky note includes a specific number (litres or cm³) or the formula V = ⅓πr²h — not just a vague statement. A 'What we still wonder' note that references the bucket/frustum indicates readiness for Lesson 3. Collect 5–6 sticky notes from learners who said least during the lesson to gauge silent learners' understanding.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners retrieve the cumulative diagram they started in Lesson 1 (a side-by-side sketch of the three Kericho containers: cylinder, cone, and bucket). Today they add three pieces of information to the diagram: (a) the formula V = ⅓πr²h written inside or beside the cone, (b) the calculated capacity '≈ 19.4 L' labelled on the conical cover, and (c) a double-headed arrow between the cone and the cylinder labelled '×3' to show the ratio. Learners also add a question-mark annotation on the bucket: 'V = ? (more than cone, less than cylinder)'. This partial model will be updated in every subsequent lesson until the frustum formula is derived in Lesson 4.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Get out the diagram you started in Lesson 1. Today you are going to make it more precise — add the formula, the calculated number, and the ratio arrow. You have 4 minutes.' Circulate and check that the ×3 arrow is placed correctly (from cone to cylinder, not the reverse). Ask one learner: 'If I drew another arrow pointing from the cylinder back to the cone, what fraction would I write on it?' (Expected answer: ⅓.) After 4 minutes, display a model diagram on the board and say: 'Your diagram should look something like this. The question mark on the bucket is the most important thing on your whole page — that is the mystery we are solving together over the next four lessons.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative annotated model (Visualising Mathematical Relationships): progressively adding quantitative and formulaic information to a single persistent diagram builds a coherent mental model of how the three shapes relate. The deliberate question-mark annotation on the frustum maintains productive inquiry tension and connects every lesson to the overarching driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: the diagram shows the correct formula V = ⅓πr²h on the cone, a numerically correct capacity label (within rounding), and the ×3 ratio arrow pointing from cone to cylinder. A question-mark annotation on the bucket indicates the learner understands the frustum is the remaining puzzle. Collect 4 diagrams at the end of the lesson as a formative artefact to review before Lesson 3.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider: (1) During the pouring demonstration, did all learners have a clear line of sight to the water level, or should the cylinder be placed on a raised surface next time? (2) How many learners predicted '3' before the demonstration — and did those who predicted otherwise show genuine surprise? Surprise is a sign of authentic inquiry; if most learners already knew the answer, consider whether this group is ready to move to pyramids faster. (3) Were learners able to distinguish between radius and diameter when substituting into V = ⅓πr²h? Errors here are diagnostic of a gap from Junior School work on circles that will compound in Lessons 3–5. (4) Review the sticky notes from the DQB: do learners' 'What we still wonder' questions specifically mention the bucket/frustum shape, or are they still focused on the cone–cylinder comparison? If fewer than half mention the frustum, spend 5 minutes at the start of Lesson 3 re-reading the driving question aloud and pointing to the bucket explicitly. (5) Did the real-world connection to the Kericho Tea Development Authority feel genuine to learners, or did it feel artificially inserted? Ask two learners informally after class.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners filled a cone with water and poured it into a matching cylinder three times, directly observing that the cylinder was exactly full after the third pour — demonstrating V(cylinder) = 3 × V(cone) using containers that represent the Kericho tea-farmer drum and conical sisal cover.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Learners derived the cone volume formula V = ⅓πr²h algebraically from the observed 1:3 ratio, calculated the capacity of the Kericho conical cover (r = 21 cm, h = 42 cm) as approximately 19 373 cm³ ≈ 19.4 litres, and confirmed it holds exactly one-third the volume of the matching cylindrical drum.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Learners explained in writing why the conical sisal cover holds far less water than the cylindrical drum despite identical height and opening width, and updated their cumulative container diagram with the formula, the calculated capacity, and a ×3 ratio arrow — leaving a deliberate question mark on the metal bucket (frustum) as the next mathematical puzzle to solve.

LESSONS.title: Volume of Pyramids: Unlocking the One-Third Relationship

slo.purpose: Learners establish and apply the formula V = ⅓ × base area × height for square-based pyramids by physically comparing pyramid and cuboid models, then use the formula to compute volumes and capacities of pyramidal grain stores — building the mathematical bridge between the cone-cylinder relationship (Lesson 1) and the frustum (Lessons 5–7).
slo.knowledge: Learners determine the volume and capacity of pyramids using the formula V(pyramid) = ⅓ × base area × height, and convert between volume units (cm³, m³) and capacity units (litres, millilitres).
slo.skills: Learners measure dimensions of pyramid and cuboid models, substitute values into the volume formula, perform unit conversions, and compare computed capacities with Lesson 1 predictions recorded on the Driving Question Board.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that the mathematical relationship between a pyramid and a cuboid mirrors the cone-cylinder relationship, recognising that elegant patterns in geometry have practical value for Kenyan farmers designing storage containers.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is the knowledge of volume and capacity useful?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1, learners predicted why the cylindrical drum holds three times the water of the conical cover. In Lesson 2, they confirmed V(cone) = ⅓ × V(cylinder). Now in Lesson 3, they discover that the exact same one-third relationship exists between a square-based pyramid and its surrounding cuboid — deepening the pattern and preparing them to later 'slice' a frustum from a pyramid (Lesson 5). This lesson also introduces grain-store pyramids as a second Kenyan context alongside the Kericho tea-farmer containers.
slo.safetyNotes: Learners handle rulers, scissors and card-stock when constructing or measuring models. Remind learners to pass scissors handle-first and to keep cutting surfaces flat on the desk. Water used in any volume-by-displacement demonstration should be in a stable, low-sided tray to avoid spillage on exercise books.

LESSONS.overview: Learners open with a quick written prediction connecting today's pyramid to the cone-cylinder pattern from Lesson 2. They then gather evidence using a hands-on pair activity: a card-stock square-based pyramid and a cuboid of identical base and height are filled with sand/rice to prove V(pyramid) = ⅓ × V(cuboid) = ⅓ × base area × height. In the Explain phase, learners apply the formula to three pyramidal grain-store problems set in the Rift Valley, computing volumes in cm³/m³ and converting to litres. They compare their computed capacities with their Lesson 1 DQB predictions, annotate errors, and close by adding two new 'How do we know…?' questions to the board. The lesson ends with a Model Building entry in which learners revise their Lesson 2 proportional diagram to include the pyramid-cuboid trio alongside the cone-cylinder trio.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners receive a half-page prompt card showing a sketch of a square-based pyramid and its enclosing cuboid (same base dimensions and height), both labelled with base side s = 12 cm and height h = 15 cm. Working individually and silently for 3 minutes, they write two predictions in their exercise books: (a) 'What fraction of the cuboid's volume do you think the pyramid holds? Give a reason linked to what we learned about cones and cylinders.' (b) 'If the cuboid holds 120 litres of grain, predict how many litres the pyramid holds.' After 3 minutes, learners share predictions with a shoulder partner for 2 minutes, then the teacher cold-calls 4 learners to share with the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute prompt cards face-down. Say: 'Turn your card over. You have 3 minutes — silent, individual thinking. Write your prediction AND your reason. I am looking for a connection to what we proved last lesson about cones and cylinders.' Start a visible 3-minute timer. Circulate and read over shoulders; note 2 learners who wrote 'one-third' and 2 who wrote a different fraction — you will cold-call all four. After 3 minutes say: 'Share with your shoulder partner for 2 minutes — convince each other.' After partner talk, say: 'I am going to hear from four people. Amina — what did you predict and why? [WAIT 12 seconds.] Thank you. James — do you agree or disagree with Amina? [WAIT 10 seconds.]' Cold-call 4 learners total. Record predictions in two columns on the board: 'One-third camp' and 'Other fraction camp'. Do NOT confirm or deny. Say: 'Let us gather evidence to settle this.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with Justified Reasoning — learners are required to anchor their numeric prediction to a causal reason (the cone-cylinder pattern), activating prior knowledge and creating a cognitive need to test the claim. Recording two 'camps' on the board makes the disagreement visible and motivates the evidence phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: learner has written a numeric prediction (fraction or litre value) AND a written reason that references either 'one-third', 'cone', or 'cylinder'. Teacher scans exercise books during circulation; learners who have only a number with no reason are prompted: 'Add one sentence — why do you think that?'

framework.learnerExperience: Pairs receive one pre-made open-top card-stock square-based pyramid and one open-top cuboid of identical base (10 cm × 10 cm) and height (12 cm), plus a cup of dry rice/sand and a 250 ml measuring jug. Step 1 (5 min): Pairs fill the pyramid level-full with rice, then pour it into the cuboid. They repeat and tally how many full pyramids of rice it takes to fill the cuboid completely. Step 2 (5 min): Pairs record their tally, compute the cuboid volume (V = l × w × h = 10 × 10 × 12 = 1 200 cm³) and use their tally to write the fraction pyramid/cuboid. Step 3 (5 min): Pairs measure their pyramid's base side and height with a ruler, then use V = ⅓ × s² × h to compute the theoretical pyramid volume and compare with the experimental fraction. Step 4 (5 min): Each pair reads 'Grain-store card A' — a diagram of a pyramidal grain store used in Eldoret with base 3 m × 3 m and height 2.4 m — and uses the formula to calculate the volume in m³ and convert to litres (1 m³ = 1 000 litres). Pairs record all steps in a structured 'Evidence Table' on a printed worksheet.
framework.teacherMoves: Before distributing materials say: 'You are going to do what scientists do — let the physical world tell us the answer. Your job is to fill carefully and count carefully. No spilling.' Distribute kits. After 2 minutes of filling say: 'Pause. Look at your tally so far. Whisper to your partner: is the pyramid going to need more or fewer fills than you predicted?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] Continue circulating. When most pairs have completed 3 fills say: 'If you have filled three times and the cuboid is not yet full, what does that tell you? [WAIT 12 seconds.] Keep going.' After Step 2, pause the class: 'Hands up — who got exactly 3 fills?' [Count hands aloud.] 'Who got close to 3 but not exactly — what might cause that?' [Cold-call 2 learners, WAIT 10 seconds each.] After Step 3 say: 'Compare your experimental fraction with your formula fraction. Are they the same? If not, write one sentence explaining why.' After Step 4 say: 'Now connect this to our Kericho farmers. The tea-farmer uses a conical cover and the Eldoret grain-store is a pyramid. What do these two shapes have in common mathematically?' [Cold-call 2 learners, WAIT 12 seconds each.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Hands-On Physical Modelling with Formula Verification — the concrete rice-filling activity generates experiential data (3 fills = one-third), which learners then reconcile with the algebraic formula. The two-step approach (experimental → formula) builds conceptual understanding before procedural fluency, preventing formula-as-magic-rule thinking.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Learner's Evidence Table shows a tally of 3 (±0.2 tolerance noted) and the fraction ⅓ written explicitly. (2) Learner has correctly computed V(cuboid) = 1 200 cm³ and V(pyramid) = 400 cm³ from the formula. (3) Grain-store card A: learner has written V = ⅓ × 9 × 2.4 = 7.2 m³ = 7 200 litres. Teacher checks Step 4 answers by circulating and initialling correct work before the class moves on.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of four on three tiered application problems, all set in Kenyan contexts. Problem 1 (Accessible): A pyramidal heap-cover used by tea pickers in Kericho has a square base of side 80 cm and a height of 60 cm. Calculate its volume in cm³ and convert to litres. Problem 2 (Standard): A grain store in Kisumu is built in the shape of a square pyramid with base 4 m × 4 m and height 3 m. The farmer wants to store 20 m³ of maize. How many such stores does she need? Problem 3 (Extended): A community in the Rift Valley uses two pyramidal stores: Store A has base 2.5 m × 2.5 m and height 3.6 m; Store B has base 3 m × 3 m and height 2 m. Which store holds more githeri (dry beans and maize)? By how many litres? Each group attempts all three, then one group presents Problem 2 and another presents Problem 3 to the class. Presenters must say: 'Our formula is…', 'We substituted…', and 'Our answer means that in the context of the farmer…'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'These three problems are all about Kenyan farmers storing food. Every calculation you do must end with a sentence that means something to a real farmer — not just a number.' Set a 12-minute group work timer. Circulate to Problem 2 groups first (most common error: forgetting to divide by 3). Prompt: 'You wrote V = 4 × 4 × 3. Is there a step missing? Look at your Evidence Table.' [WAIT 12 seconds.] For Problem 3 prompt struggling groups: 'Calculate each store separately first. Then subtract.' After 12 minutes select two groups for presentations. After each presentation ask the class: 'Do you agree with their formula substitution? Show me thumbs up, sideways or down.' [Pause 8 seconds.] Cold-call one 'sideways' learner: 'What concerns you? [WAIT 12 seconds.]' After both presentations ask the whole class: 'Look at the cone in our Kericho phenomenon and the pyramid in these problems. What is the shared mathematical secret?' [WAIT 15 seconds.] Cold-call 3 learners. Consolidate on the board: V(pyramid) = ⅓ × b² × h alongside V(cone) = ⅓ × π r² × h, circling the ⅓ in both.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Group Problem Solving with Public Presentation — tiered problems ensure all learners access the formula while the presentation requirement ('our answer means that…') forces contextualisation. Displaying V(pyramid) and V(cone) side-by-side on the board makes the structural pattern explicit, supporting transfer to frustums in later lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Problem 1: V = ⅓ × 80² × 60 = 128 000 cm³ = 128 litres — learner has shown the division-by-3 step explicitly. (2) Problem 2: V = ⅓ × 16 × 3 = 16 m³; 20 ÷ 16 = 1.25, so 2 stores needed — learner has interpreted the non-integer answer correctly in context. (3) Problem 3: Store A = 7 500 litres, Store B = 6 000 litres; A holds 1 500 litres more — learner has converted both to litres before comparing. Teacher stamps or ticks at least Problem 1 in each learner's book before the DQB phase.

framework.learnerExperience: The teacher uncovers the class DQB (begun in Lesson 1). Learners spend 3 minutes silently re-reading all current sticky notes. They then open their Lesson 1 prediction notebooks and compare their original guesses about the Kericho containers with what they now know from Lessons 1–3. Each learner writes on two sticky notes: (i) One 'We now know…' statement — something today's lesson confirmed or corrected from their Lesson 1 prediction. (ii) One 'We still need to figure out…' question — a gap that today's evidence did not yet answer (e.g., 'We know cone = ⅓ cylinder and pyramid = ⅓ cuboid, but how does the metal bucket — a frustum — fit this pattern?'). Learners post notes in the appropriate DQB columns. The teacher reads 3–4 new questions aloud and asks the class to vote (hands) on which question they most want to answer next.
framework.teacherMoves: Uncover the DQB. Say: 'Take 3 minutes — read every note on this board. Think about how today's lesson changes or confirms what is already here.' [Set 3-minute timer, enforce silence.] After 3 minutes: 'Open your Lesson 1 prediction page. What did you predict then? What do you know now? Write your two sticky notes.' [Allow 4 minutes.] Circulate and prompt learners whose 'We still need to figure out…' note is too vague (e.g., 'more about frustums'): 'Can you make it more specific — what exactly about the frustum puzzles you?' After posting, read 4 selected notes aloud. For each: 'Who agrees this is our next big question? [Hands.]' Highlight the winning question with a star sticker. Say: 'That starred question is exactly where Lessons 5, 6 and 7 will take us. Keep it in mind.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict–Confirm–Question Cycle on the DQB — revisiting Lesson 1 predictions against Lesson 3 evidence makes learning progression visible to learners. The 'We still need to figure out…' notes sustain epistemic curiosity and give learners authorship over the unit's investigative direction, increasing engagement in subsequent lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Learner's 'We now know…' note references a specific numerical relationship (e.g., 'one-third', '⅓ × base area × height') rather than a vague statement. (2) Learner's 'We still need to figure out…' note names the frustum or the metal bucket from the phenomenon. Teacher photographs the updated DQB at end of lesson for the class digital portfolio.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the proportional diagram they built in Lesson 2 (a cylinder and cone drawn to scale showing the 3:1 volume ratio). They now extend that diagram by drawing a cuboid and its enclosed pyramid (same proportions) directly beside the cone-cylinder pair, labelling both with the ⅓ relationship. Below both pairs they write: 'Pattern: Pointed shape = ⅓ × surrounding box, whether the base is a circle (cone) or a square (pyramid).' They then annotate the Kericho phenomenon image (printed on the worksheet) by drawing a dashed arrow from the metal bucket (frustum) with the label: 'NEXT: frustum = pyramid − smaller pyramid? Volume still to be determined.' Learners share their revised model with a partner for 2 minutes, giving one specific piece of praise and one question.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute Lesson 2 diagrams (returned or re-drawn from notes). Say: 'Your model so far shows cones and cylinders. Today we add a new pair to the family — pyramid and cuboid. Draw them beside your existing pair and label the ⅓ relationship.' [Allow 6 minutes.] Circulate; prompt: 'Make sure your pyramid and cuboid are drawn to the same scale ratio as your cone and cylinder — does your drawing show the pyramid is clearly smaller than the cuboid?' After 6 minutes: 'Now look at the metal bucket — the frustum — in our Kericho picture. Add that dashed arrow. What question does your arrow ask?' [Allow 3 minutes.] Pair share for 2 minutes: 'One praise, one question — be specific.' Cold-call 2 learners to share their partner's question: 'What question did your partner write on their arrow? [WAIT 10 seconds.]' Close: 'Your model is growing. Every lesson we add one more piece. By Lesson 7 your model will explain exactly why the metal bucket holds more than the cone but less than the cylinder — and you will be able to calculate exactly how much more.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Annotated Model Revision — learners physically extend a growing visual model across lessons, making cross-lesson knowledge integration tangible. The dashed arrow pointing to the frustum creates a forward-looking knowledge gap that primes learners for Lessons 5–7, reinforcing the unit's narrative coherence and the anchoring phenomenon's unresolved element.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (1) Learner's model shows both pairs (cone-cylinder AND pyramid-cuboid) with the ⅓ label on both. (2) The written pattern statement uses the words 'pointed shape', '⅓', and either 'circle' or 'square' as the base descriptor. (3) The dashed arrow to the frustum is present and labelled with a question (not just 'frustum'). Teacher collects models at the end of the lesson to review overnight and return with written feedback before Lesson 4.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, consider the following questions: (1) During the rice-filling activity, did all pairs obtain close to 3 fills? If several groups got 2 or 4 fills, what procedural issues (overfilling, poorly constructed models) should be addressed before Lesson 5? (2) In the Explain phase, did learners consistently write the ÷3 step explicitly, or did many jump from V = b² × h to the answer? If the latter, plan a short starter in Lesson 4 where learners must annotate a worked example showing every step. (3) Looking at the DQB notes: did learners' 'We still need to figure out…' questions point toward the frustum, or are there unexpected gaps (e.g., confusion about volume vs capacity units) that need to be addressed before moving to Lesson 4? (4) Which learners have not yet connected today's pyramid result back to the Kericho metal bucket? Identify them by name for targeted questioning in the next lesson's Predict Phase. (5) Were the three application problems appropriately tiered? If most groups did not reach Problem 3, consider whether Problem 2 needs scaffolding (e.g., a partially completed formula) in future iterations.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners filled a card-stock square-based pyramid with rice and poured it into an identical-base-and-height cuboid, repeating until the cuboid was full. They recorded that it took 3 full pyramids to fill 1 cuboid, and used a ruler to measure the base and height of their pyramid model.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: V(pyramid) = ⅓ × base area × height; the same one-third relationship that links a cone to its cylinder also links a square-based pyramid to its cuboid. Learners also practised converting pyramid volumes from cm³ and m³ into litres (1 m³ = 1 000 litres) using grain-store problems from Eldoret, Kisumu, and the Rift Valley.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The one-third factor in both V(cone) = ⅓ × πr² × h and V(pyramid) = ⅓ × b² × h reflects a geometric pattern: any pointed solid (apex tapering to a point) holds exactly one-third of its surrounding box, regardless of whether the base is circular or square. This explains why the pyramidal grain stores used by Kenyan farmers hold far less grain than a similarly sized cuboid store — and raises the question of how to compute the volume of the frustum-shaped metal bucket, which lies between these two extremes.
