LESSONS.title: Introducing Frustums of Cones: Deriving the Volume Formula and Solving the Bucket Mystery

slo.purpose: Learners derive the volume formula for a frustum of a cone by reasoning from the cone-cylinder relationship established in earlier lessons, then apply it to calculate the exact capacity of the Kericho tea farmers' metal bucket — resolving the anchoring phenomenon.
slo.knowledge: Learners should be able to: (a) determine the volume and capacity of a frustum of a cone; (b) derive V(frustum) = ⅓π h(R² + Rr + r²) by subtracting the small cone from the large cone; (c) apply volume and capacity of frustums in real-life situations.
slo.skills: Measuring dimensions of a frustum (top radius R, bottom radius r, slant height, vertical height h); substituting values into the frustum-of-cone formula; converting between cm³ and litres; comparing capacities of different containers; communicating mathematical reasoning step by step.
slo.attitudes: Appreciate the power of mathematical derivation in explaining everyday observations; show curiosity about why similar-looking containers hold different amounts; value precision in measurement and calculation; respect peers' reasoning during collaborative derivation.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is the knowledge of volume and capacity useful?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–3 learners established that a cone holds exactly one-third of a same-dimension cylinder, and calculated volumes of cones and pyramids. Lesson 4 now tackles the third container in the phenomenon — the metal frustum bucket. Learners physically measure the bucket, reconstruct the full cone from which it was cut, subtract volumes, and arrive at V = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²). This is the mathematical climax that explains why the bucket holds more than the cone but less than the cylinder, fully resolving the anchoring phenomenon.
slo.safetyNotes: Ensure water is cleaned up immediately if spilled during hands-on measurement to prevent slipping. Handle metal bucket edges with care — inspect for sharp rims before passing to learners. Use non-breakable measuring containers only.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by predicting where the frustum bucket's capacity sits relative to the cone and cylinder using their prior knowledge. They then measure a real frustum-shaped bucket (top radius R, bottom radius r, vertical height h) in groups, reconstruct the dimensions of the full cone from which it was cut using similar-triangle reasoning, and derive V(frustum) = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²) step by step. Using this formula they calculate the bucket's capacity in litres, compare it to the cylinder and cone results from Lessons 1–3, and fully resolve the anchoring phenomenon. The lesson closes with learners revising their cumulative class model and Driving Question Board to capture the complete three-container relationship.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner individually examines a diagram showing the three Kericho containers (cylinder, cone, frustum bucket) — all with the same height of 30 cm and the same top opening diameter of 28 cm — alongside a partially completed capacity table from Lessons 1–3. The table shows: Cylinder ≈ 18.47 L, Cone ≈ 6.16 L. The Frustum row is blank. Learners write a personal prediction: 'I predict the frustum bucket holds approximately ___ litres because ___.' They are also asked to sketch what the full cone might look like if the frustum were 'completed' downward, labelling where the tip of the cone would be.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the three-container diagram on the board (or hold up the physical containers). Say: 'Look at these three containers that Kamau and Atieno's tea farm uses in Kericho. We have calculated two of them. Today we settle the mystery of the bucket.' Hand out the prediction worksheet. Allow 3 minutes of silent individual thinking. After 3 minutes say: 'Write your prediction and your reason — even if you are not sure, commit to a number.' After writing, cold-call 4 learners to share predictions (select one who said 'closer to the cone', one 'closer to the cylinder', one 'exactly in the middle', and one who used a fraction argument). Record all four predictions visibly on the board under the heading 'OUR PREDICTIONS — we will check these at the end.' Do NOT confirm or reject any prediction. Say: 'Keep these in mind — your evidence today will tell you who was right.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Anchored Prediction with Boundary Constraints — learners use the established cone (⅓ cylinder) relationship as a lower bound and the cylinder as an upper bound to reason that the frustum must lie between the two values. This activates prior knowledge from Lessons 1–3 and creates cognitive need for the derivation.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Learner's written prediction includes (1) a numerical estimate between 6.16 L and 18.47 L and (2) a written justification referencing the cone-cylinder relationship or the physical appearance of the frustum. Teacher scans 6–8 predictions during the 3-minute window. Flag any learner who predicts outside the 6–16 L range for targeted questioning in Phase 2.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4 receive one metal bucket (frustum-shaped), a ruler, a tape measure, and a recording sheet. They measure: top inner diameter (D), bottom inner diameter (d), and vertical height h. They convert to radii: R = D/2, r = d/2. They record raw measurements and compare with two neighbouring groups. Then learners watch a 4-minute teacher-guided demonstration: the teacher places the frustum bucket next to a tall cone model (made from card) that has the same top radius and same slant angle. The teacher tilts the cone to show it could be 'completed' downward to a tip. Learners observe where the tip of the full cone would be relative to the bucket's bottom. They record: 'The full cone is taller than the bucket. The small cone cut away is shorter. Together, large cone = frustum + small cone.'
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute equipment and say: 'You have 6 minutes to measure your bucket carefully. Measure top diameter, bottom diameter, and vertical height. Record in your table. Each person in the group must independently record — do not share one answer.' Circulate and check at least 4 groups. After 6 minutes, cold-call 3 groups to report their R, r, h values. Write them on the board. If values differ by more than 0.5 cm ask: 'What might cause the difference? How do engineers handle measurement uncertainty?' (WAIT TIME: 12 seconds.) Then hold up the cone model. Say: 'This cone has the same opening — radius 14 cm — as the bucket. Watch what happens when I place it inside.' Slowly lower the cone into the frustum outline drawn on the board. Ask: 'What solid is left inside the cone but outside the bucket?' (WAIT TIME: 10 seconds.) Cold-call 2 learners. Guide to the answer: 'a smaller cone at the bottom.' Say: 'That is our key observation. Write it in your books: Large cone = Frustum + Small cone. Therefore Frustum = Large cone − Small cone.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concrete–Pictorial–Abstract (CPA) Sequence — learners first handle physical objects (concrete measurement), then observe the cone-within-frustum demonstration (pictorial/representational), and will move to algebra in Phase 3 (abstract). Naming the strategy aloud helps learners track where they are in the reasoning chain.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Each group's recording sheet shows three distinct measurements (R, r, h) with units. Learners can verbally state 'Large cone = Frustum + Small cone' when cold-called. Teacher listens for incorrect identification of slant height as vertical height — correct immediately with: 'We need the perpendicular height, not the slant. How would you measure that carefully?'

framework.learnerExperience: Guided derivation in pairs. Learners are given a printed diagram of the large cone (height H, radius R) with the small cone (height H−h, radius r) shaded inside it. They work through five scaffolded steps written on the board: Step 1 — Write V(large cone) in terms of H and R. Step 2 — Use similar triangles to show H/R = (H−h)/r, then solve for H to get H = Rh/(R−r). Step 3 — Write V(small cone) in terms of (H−h) and r. Step 4 — Subtract: V(frustum) = V(large) − V(small) = ⅓πR²H − ⅓πr²(H−h). Step 5 — Substitute H = Rh/(R−r), expand, simplify algebraically to reach V = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²). Pairs then substitute their measured bucket values to calculate volume in cm³ and convert to litres (÷ 1000). They also calculate the percentage of the cylinder's capacity that the bucket holds.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'We observed that V(frustum) = V(large cone) − V(small cone). Now we will use algebra to turn that observation into a formula we can use for any frustum.' Write Step 1 on the board and pause. 'Write V(large cone). Everyone.' (WAIT TIME: 10 seconds.) Cold-call 1 learner for the answer. Affirm: 'Good — ⅓πR²H. But we don't know H yet — that is what Step 2 solves.' Work through the similar-triangle argument carefully: draw the two right triangles on the board, label R, r, H, H−h. Ask: 'Why are these two triangles similar?' (WAIT TIME: 12 seconds.) Cold-call 2 learners — listen for 'same apex angle' or 'same slant direction.' After deriving H = Rh/(R−r), say: 'This is the most important algebraic step. Copy it, box it.' Steps 4 and 5 — work one line at a time, pausing for pairs to verify each line. At Step 5 say: 'This formula — one-third pi h, bracket, R-squared plus R-r plus r-squared — is the formula for ANY frustum of a cone. Add it to your formula card.' Then say: 'Now substitute your group's measured values. Calculate the bucket's volume in cm³, then convert to litres.' Allow 8 minutes for calculation. Cold-call 3 groups to share their answers. Circle back to the phenomenon: 'So where does the bucket sit — closer to the cone at 6.16 L or the cylinder at 18.47 L? Why does it sit there mathematically?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Step-by-Step Algebraic Derivation with Sense-Checks — rather than presenting the formula as a rule to memorise, each algebraic step is derived and sense-checked against the physical model. This builds understanding of WHY the formula has three terms (R², Rr, r²) — they arise naturally from expansion. The strategy explicitly connects symbolic manipulation to the physical phenomenon of 'cutting' a small cone from a large one.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Learners' worked derivation in exercise books shows all 5 steps with correct algebraic manipulation, particularly the similar-triangle step H = Rh/(R−r) and the final simplified form. Teacher checks 5 books during the 8-minute calculation window. Success threshold: at least 4 of 5 books show a final volume between 10 L and 15 L for typical bucket dimensions (R≈14 cm, r≈9 cm, h≈30 cm). Flag pairs whose answer is outside this range for immediate peer-check.

framework.learnerExperience: Whole-class DQB update (10 minutes). The class Driving Question Board displays three columns: WHAT WE OBSERVED | WHAT WE NOW KNOW | WHAT WE STILL WONDER. Learners write new sticky-note contributions: column 2 entries include 'V(frustum) = ⅓πh(R²+Rr+r²)', 'Bucket holds ≈ [X] L — more than cone, less than cylinder', 'The formula comes from subtracting cones — it has THREE terms because of (R+r)(R²−Rr+r²) factoring… or from the expansion.' Column 3 entries (wonder questions) might include: 'Can we derive a formula for a frustum of a square pyramid the same way?', 'What if R = r — does the formula give a cylinder? Let's check!', 'How do engineers who design KPLC water tanks use this?'. The completed capacity table now shows all three containers: Cone 6.16 L → Frustum ≈ 12.3 L → Cylinder 18.47 L.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take two sticky notes. On the first, write one thing you now KNOW that you didn't know at the start of this lesson — make it mathematical. On the second, write one question you still have or something you wonder about.' Allow 3 minutes of silent writing. Then invite learners to bring their notes to the board. Read 4 'know' notes and 4 'wonder' notes aloud. For one wonder note that says 'What if R = r?' say: 'Let's test it right now — substitute R = r into our formula.' (WAIT TIME: 15 seconds.) Cold-call 1 learner to work it on the board — the formula should collapse to ⅓π h(3r²) = πr²h, which is the cylinder formula. Say: 'Does that make sense? When the top and bottom radii are equal, a frustum IS a cylinder.' Point to the driving question on the board and say: 'Our driving question asks HOW we can design a container to hold exactly the capacity we need. What does today's formula give us the power to do?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Know–Wonder Board Protocol — separating 'what we know' from 'what we still wonder' externalises metacognitive awareness and shows learners that mathematical understanding is cumulative and ongoing. The live check (R=r gives cylinder) models mathematical sense-making as verification through special cases, a key NGSS practice of 'Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking.'
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: 'Know' sticky notes contain mathematically precise statements (formula written correctly, numerical result for the bucket stated in litres). 'Wonder' notes show genuine extension thinking beyond the lesson content. Teacher screens notes for misconceptions — e.g., a note saying 'frustum always holds half of the cylinder' is flagged and gently corrected publicly: 'That's an interesting conjecture — let's test it with our numbers. Does our bucket hold half of 18.47 L?'

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually update their cumulative Capacity Model — a labelled diagram they have been building across Lessons 1–4. They add the frustum bucket with full dimensions, the derived formula, and the calculated capacity. They draw a three-container comparison bar (like a capacity bar chart) showing Cone : Frustum : Cylinder in correct proportion. They annotate: 'The frustum holds more than the cone because it has a wider base — it retains the bottom width of the large cone but discards the narrow tip where volume is least.' Finally, learners respond to the Exit Prompt in writing: 'A different tea farm in Kericho uses a frustum bucket with R = 15 cm, r = 10 cm, h = 35 cm. Calculate its capacity in litres to 2 decimal places. Would you recommend this bucket or the one we measured today for carrying more tea leaves? Justify your answer mathematically.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your Capacity Models from Lessons 1 to 3. We are adding our third and final container today.' Give learners 5 minutes to draw, label, and annotate. Circulate and check that the formula is written correctly and the bar chart proportions are roughly accurate (frustum bar should be about 2/3 of cylinder bar). After 5 minutes say: 'Now the exit task — this is individual. You have 7 minutes.' Read the prompt aloud once. Remind learners: 'Show every substitution step — do not just write the answer.' After 7 minutes, collect written responses. Before dismissing, point to the three containers one final time and say: 'At the start of this unit, Kamau and Atieno's farm workers were puzzled — same height, same opening, very different amounts. Can you now explain this to a Form 1 student in one sentence?' (WAIT TIME: 12 seconds.) Cold-call 2 learners for their one-sentence explanations. Close with: 'Next lesson we extend this to frustums of pyramids — the principle is identical, but the base shape changes.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision — learners physically add to a model they have built over four lessons, making the growth of their understanding visible and tangible. The proportional capacity bar chart forces quantitative reasoning about relative sizes. The exit prompt applies the formula to a novel Kenyan context, assessing transfer. This reflects the NGSS practice of 'Developing and Using Models' as an ongoing scientific and mathematical activity.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator (model): Frustum diagram is correctly labelled with R, r, h, formula, and capacity in litres. Bar chart shows frustum between cone and cylinder with approximately correct proportions. Observable indicator (exit prompt): Learner correctly substitutes R=15, r=10, h=35 into V = ⅓π(35)(15²+15×10+10²) = ⅓π(35)(225+150+100) = ⅓π(35)(475) ≈ 17,495 cm³ ≈ 17.50 L. Recommendation is justified by comparing to the class bucket's volume. Success threshold: correct formula application and answer in range 17.40–17.60 L. Teacher reviews exit prompts before Lesson 5 to identify learners who need re-teaching of the similar-triangle H derivation.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
After collecting exit prompts, review these three questions before Lesson 5:
1. FORMULA DERIVATION: What percentage of learners correctly wrote V = ⅓πh(R²+Rr+r²) without copying from a neighbour? If fewer than 70% did so independently, open Lesson 5 with a 5-minute paired re-derivation from scratch before moving to pyramid frustums.
2. SIMILAR-TRIANGLE STEP: Which learners struggled to accept H = Rh/(R−r)? This algebraic manipulation requires comfort with literal equations. Prepare a visual proof using two nested cone diagrams for those learners.
3. PHENOMENON CONNECTION: Did learners' one-sentence closing explanations reference both shape (geometry) and quantity (formula/numbers)? A purely geometric explanation ('the cone has a pointy tip') without quantitative support suggests learners have intuition but not yet mathematical precision — plan a short 'convince me with numbers' challenge at the start of Lesson 5.
Also reflect: Was the 80-minute period sufficient for the full derivation AND the exit prompt? If the derivation ran long, consider separating Step 5 (algebraic expansion) into a structured homework task so that Lesson 4 class time focuses on measurement, the key subtraction insight, and the formula application.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners physically measured a frustum-shaped metal bucket (top radius R, bottom radius r, vertical height h) and observed a cone model placed alongside it, noticing that the frustum is a large cone with a small cone removed from the bottom.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Learners derived V(frustum of cone) = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²) by subtracting V(small cone) from V(large cone), using similar-triangle reasoning to eliminate the unknown full height H. They calculated the Kericho bucket's capacity in litres and placed it correctly between the cone (~6.16 L) and the cylinder (~18.47 L), resolving the anchoring phenomenon.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The frustum bucket holds more water than the cone because removing the narrow tip of the cone discards very little volume — the tip contributes almost nothing — while retaining the wide bottom section. The three terms R², Rr, r² in the formula arise algebraically from expanding the subtraction of two cone volumes and reflect the interplay between the large radius, the small radius, and their geometric mean. This is why containers of the same height and top diameter can hold dramatically different amounts depending on their shape.

LESSONS.aresKeywords: frustum of cone, volume of frustum, capacity, V = ⅓πh(R²+Rr+r²), cone subtraction, similar triangles, Kericho tea, metal bucket, cone volume, cylinder volume, derivation, measurement, litres, cubic centimetres, Kenya Grade 10, Essential Mathematics, Sub-Strand 2.7

LESSONS.title: Volume of Frustums of Pyramids — Designing the Perfect Grain-Storage Bin

slo.purpose: To extend the frustum concept from cones to square and rectangular pyramidal frustums, and to apply the formula V = ⅓h(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)) in computing the volume and capacity of a pyramidal grain-storage bin in litres and kilograms of maize.
slo.knowledge: The learner knows that: (a) a frustum of a pyramid is formed by cutting a pyramid with a plane parallel to its base; (b) the volume of a frustum of a pyramid is given by V = ⅓h(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)), where A₁ and A₂ are the areas of the two parallel faces and h is the perpendicular height between them; (c) 1 litre = 1 000 cm³; and (d) mass = volume × density, enabling conversion of capacity in litres to kilograms of maize (density ≈ 0.72 kg/litre).
slo.skills: The learner is able to: (a) identify the two parallel faces and the perpendicular height of a pyramidal frustum; (b) compute the areas A₁ and A₂ for square and rectangular bases; (c) substitute correctly into V = ⅓h(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)) and evaluate the expression step by step; (d) convert the volume in cm³ to litres; (e) calculate the mass of maize the bin can hold using density; (f) update their cumulative DQB model to include pyramidal frustums alongside conical frustums, cylinders, and cones.
slo.attitudes: The learner appreciates that mathematical formulas are practical tools for solving real-world design challenges faced by Kenyan farmers, and values precision in calculation as a form of respect for the needs of the community.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is the knowledge of volume and capacity useful?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–4 learners established that V_cylinder = πr²h, V_cone = ⅓πr²h, and V_frustum(cone) = ⅓πh(r₁² + r₂² + r₁r₂). Today they discover that the same structural logic — the average of two base areas weighted by the geometric mean — extends to pyramidal frustums. By computing the capacity of a square-based pyramidal grain-storage bin used in Kericho and Rift Valley farms, and converting that capacity to kilograms of maize, learners move from the tea-leaf containers of the anchoring phenomenon to a broader class of frustum shapes, deepening their answer to the driving question: the shape of a frustum's cross-section (circular or rectangular) changes A₁ and A₂ but leaves the volume formula structurally identical.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials are used. If physical cardboard models are assembled, learners should take care with scissors and craft knives; these should only be handled under teacher supervision. Ensure adequate desk space so that 3-D models are not knocked over.

LESSONS.overview: Lesson 5 of 8 builds directly on Lesson 4's treatment of conical frustums. The anchoring phenomenon is revisited: the Kericho tea farmers' metal bucket (a conical frustum) is now compared to a square-based pyramidal bin used to store harvested maize in the Rift Valley. Learners first predict whether the pyramidal bin holds more or less than the conical frustum of similar dimensions, then observe a worked derivation linking the pyramid-frustum formula to the cone-frustum formula they already know. They explain and apply the formula V = ⅓h(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)) to a realistic grain-bin design problem, convert the result to litres and kilograms of maize, and finally update both their Driving Question Board and their cumulative cross-section model to include pyramidal frustums. The lesson reinforces the KICD-mandated competencies of critical thinking, creativity, and unity while embedding financial-literacy and food-security PCIs.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners are shown two side-by-side scale drawings on the board: (A) the Kericho tea-farmers' metal bucket from the anchoring phenomenon — a conical frustum with top radius r₁ = 14 cm, bottom radius r₂ = 9 cm, height h = 30 cm — and (B) a square-based pyramidal maize-storage bin with top square side a₁ = 26 cm, bottom square side a₂ = 18 cm, and the same height h = 30 cm. Learners individually write a prediction in their exercise books: 'Which container holds more, and by how much? Explain your reasoning in at least two sentences.' They then share with a shoulder partner for 2 minutes before a whole-class cold-call.
framework.teacherMoves: Display both drawings and say: 'Look carefully at these two containers. They have the same height — 30 centimetres. I want you to silently predict which holds more water and write down WHY you think so. You have 3 minutes — go.' [Allow 3 minutes of silent individual writing.] After writing, say: 'Turn to your neighbour and compare predictions. Do you agree or disagree? You have 2 minutes.' [Allow 2 minutes.] After partner talk, say: 'Let us hear some predictions. I will cold-call — Achieng, what did you and your partner predict?' [WAIT 10 seconds after naming before prompting.] Cold-call 4 learners (aim for at least 2 different predictions). Record all predictions verbatim on a section of the board labelled 'Our Predictions — Lesson 5'. Do NOT confirm or correct yet. End by saying: 'We are going to find out exactly which is larger — and by how much — by the end of today's lesson.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Elicit-and-record predictions: by surfacing prior reasoning (area comparisons, mental estimation) before instruction, the teacher creates a cognitive anchor. Learners will compare their predictions against computed results at the end of the lesson, making the resolution of surprise a powerful sensemaking moment.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: every learner has at least two written sentences in their book before partner talk. Teacher circulates and scans for (a) learners who compare base areas (strong prior knowledge), (b) learners who only compare heights (partial understanding), and (c) learners who are unsure how to start (need scaffolding during the Observe phase). Teacher notes names for targeted cold-calling later.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners observe a three-part structured derivation displayed on the board and in their ARES workbooks. Part A (5 min): Teacher displays a whole square pyramid and its frustum cut-out, labelling A₁ (top face area), A₂ (bottom face area), and h (perpendicular height). Learners copy the diagram and label into their books. Part B (8 min): Teacher walks through the algebraic derivation of V_frustum(pyramid) = ⅓h(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)) side by side with the cone-frustum formula V = ⅓πh(r₁² + r₂² + r₁r₂), showing that both share the identical structure: ⅓ × h × (top area + bottom area + geometric mean area). Learners annotate: they colour-code matching terms in both formulas with two different coloured pens. Part C (7 min): Learners independently work through a guided numerical example in their ARES workbook — a pyramidal bin with a₁ = 20 cm, a₂ = 12 cm, h = 25 cm — filling in a structured calculation scaffold with blanks for A₁, A₂, √(A₁A₂), the sum, and the final volume.
framework.teacherMoves: Part A: Sketch the pyramid frustum slowly. Say: 'This is a frustum of a square pyramid — the shape many grain-storage bins and maize silos in the Rift Valley use. What are the two parallel faces?' [WAIT 10 seconds.] Cold-call 2 learners. Label A₁ and A₂. Say: 'h is always the perpendicular distance between the two parallel faces — not the slant height.' Underline 'perpendicular' on the board. Part B: Write both formulas on the board simultaneously. Say: 'I want you to look at the cone-frustum formula we derived in Lesson 4 — here — and the pyramid-frustum formula — here. What do you notice about their structure?' [WAIT 12 seconds.] Cold-call 3 learners. Guide learners to see the structural identity. Say: 'The formula does not care whether the base is a circle or a square — it always says: one-third times height times the sum of the top area, the bottom area, and the geometric mean of the two areas. Write that sentence in your own words under the formulas.' Part C: Say: 'Now try the guided example in your workbook on your own — you have 5 minutes. Show every step.' Circulate, checking that learners correctly compute A₁ = 20² = 400 cm², A₂ = 12² = 144 cm², √(A₁A₂) = √(400 × 144) = √57 600 = 240 cm², sum = 784 cm², V = ⅓ × 25 × 784 = 6 533.3 cm³. After 5 minutes: 'Who got 6 533 point 3 cubic centimetres? Show me a thumbs-up.' Address the most common error observed.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Side-by-side formula comparison with colour-coding: placing the cone-frustum and pyramid-frustum formulas next to each other and having learners physically colour matching terms makes the structural analogy visible and tactile, reducing cognitive load and building the generalisation that the same mathematical skeleton underlies both. This directly advances the driving question: both the bucket and the pyramidal bin obey the same volume logic.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) learners' annotations show correct colour-coding of matching terms in both formulas; (b) in Part C, learners who correctly compute √(A₁A₂) = 240 cm² are on track — teacher checks this intermediate step explicitly during circulation; (c) thumbs-up count after Part C gives a rapid whole-class gauge. If fewer than 70% of learners show thumbs-up, the teacher re-models the √(A₁A₂) step before moving to Phase 3.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of four to solve the main application problem, which is explicitly connected to the anchoring phenomenon: 'A maize farmer in Kericho uses a pyramidal grain-storage bin with a square top of side 30 cm, a square bottom of side 20 cm, and a perpendicular height of 40 cm. (a) Calculate the volume of the bin in cm³. (b) Convert the volume to litres. (c) The farmer plans to fill the bin with dry maize. Given that dry maize has a density of approximately 0.72 kg per litre, calculate the mass of maize the full bin can hold. (d) The farmer wants to double the capacity. If the height stays the same, what side length should both the top and the bottom square be scaled to? (Use the volume scale factor from Sub-Strand 2.1 — Similarity and Enlargement.)' Each group records their working on an A3 sheet. After 15 minutes of group work, two groups present their solutions to the class (teacher selects one group with a correct solution and one group that made a common error, without pre-announcing which is which). The class critiques both presentations.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the A3 problem sheet. Say: 'This is the same Kericho farming community from our anchoring phenomenon — now storing maize, not tea leaves. Work in your groups. Assign roles: one calculator, one recorder, one checker, one presenter. You have 15 minutes.' [Circulate actively. After 5 minutes, check that all groups have correctly computed A₁ = 30² = 900 cm² and A₂ = 20² = 400 cm². If a group is stuck on part (d), ask: 'In Sub-Strand 2.1 we found that if the volume scale factor is k³, and we want volume to double, what must k³ equal?' WAIT 12 seconds before offering further guidance.] After 15 minutes, say: 'Group 3, please present your working for parts (a), (b) and (c).' After Group 3 presents, say: 'Group 6, please present your working for part (d).' After both presentations, pose to the class: 'Do you agree with Group 3's answer for part (c)? Raise your hand if you got the same mass of maize.' Cold-call one learner who disagrees to explain the discrepancy. For part (d), explicitly ask: 'If volume doubles, k³ = 2, so k = ∛2 ≈ 1.26 — what does that tell us about the new side lengths?' Cold-call 2 learners. Confirm: new top side ≈ 30 × 1.26 ≈ 37.8 cm, new bottom side ≈ 20 × 1.26 ≈ 25.2 cm. Close by saying: 'Now return to our predictions from the start of the lesson. Was the pyramidal bin larger or smaller than the conical frustum? Let us check.' [Work through V_cone-frustum = ⅓π(30)(15² + 10² + 150) = ⅓π(30)(400) = 12 566 cm³ vs V_pyramid-frustum = ⅓(40)(900 + 400 + 600) = ⅓(40)(1900) = 25 333 cm³.] Say: 'The pyramidal bin holds MORE — about twice as much. How many of you predicted that? Why does it hold more even though both have the same height?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Collaborative problem-solving with cross-group critique: having two groups present — one correct, one with an error — turns the comparison into a sensemaking activity where learners must apply their emerging understanding to evaluate claims. The return to the opening predictions closes a predict-observe-explain loop within the lesson, directly connecting to the anchoring phenomenon and the driving question. Connecting part (d) to Sub-Strand 2.1 (Similarity and Enlargement) makes cross-strand mathematical coherence visible.
framework.formativeAssessment: Expected answers for formative checking: (a) A₁ = 900 cm², A₂ = 400 cm², √(A₁A₂) = 600 cm², V = ⅓ × 40 × 1900 = 25 333.3 cm³; (b) 25.33 litres; (c) 25.33 × 0.72 ≈ 18.24 kg of maize; (d) k = ∛2 ≈ 1.26, new top side ≈ 37.8 cm, new bottom side ≈ 25.2 cm. Teacher uses the A3 sheets as a visible formative record — collect all sheets at the end of class for written feedback before Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner independently writes on a sticky note (or in a designated DQB section of their workbook if physical sticky notes are unavailable): one thing they can NOW explain about the driving question that they could not explain before today, and one question that today's lesson has raised for them. Learners post or write their notes. The teacher reads out 4–5 contributions and clusters them on the DQB under two growing columns: 'What we can now explain' and 'What we still need to find out'. Learners update the DQB tracking table in their workbooks, ticking off: cylinder ✓, cone ✓, conical frustum ✓, pyramidal frustum ✓ (today), and noting that 'designing a container of exact capacity' remains the culminating challenge.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Take a sticky note — or open your workbook to the DQB page. Write: one thing you can NOW explain about why the tea farmers' containers hold different amounts, and one new question today has made you think about. You have 3 minutes — on your own, silent.' [WAIT 3 minutes.] 'Post your notes. I am going to read some aloud.' Read 4–5 notes, grouping them visibly on the board. Highlight any note that connects to the driving question — e.g., 'The formula is the same structure for any frustum — it does not matter if the base is a circle or a rectangle.' Say: 'That is a big idea. The Kericho tea farmers' bucket and the Rift Valley maize bin both obey the same mathematical rule — one-third times height times that special sum of areas. Tick pyramidal frustum in your tracking table. What is left for us to answer before we can fully design our own container?' Cold-call 2 learners. Guide towards: 'We need to know how to choose dimensions to hit an exact target capacity — that is our culminating design challenge in Lesson 8.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB update with explicit tracking table: making cumulative understanding visible on a shared board (and in individual workbooks) gives learners a metacognitive map of the unit's evidence-gathering sequence. Clustering learner-generated questions around the driving question sustains inquiry momentum and shows learners that their confusion is productive and shared.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: each learner's sticky note or workbook entry contains (a) a specific mathematical claim (not a vague statement like 'I learned about frustums') and (b) a genuine question. Teacher scans for entries that reveal lingering misconceptions — e.g., 'Is the formula different if the base is a triangle?' — and flags these for targeted attention in Lesson 6.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their cumulative cross-section model — a side-by-side annotated diagram that has been built across Lessons 1–5. Today they add a new panel: a correctly labelled cross-section of a square-based pyramidal frustum, showing A₁ (top face), A₂ (bottom face), h (perpendicular height), and the formula V = ⅓h(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)). Below the diagram they write: 'Structural link: this formula has the same form as the conical frustum formula because both express the average of two base areas weighted by their geometric mean, scaled by ⅓h.' Learners also annotate an arrow connecting the pyramidal frustum panel back to the Similarity & Enlargement panel, showing how the volume scale factor (k³ = 2 → k = ∛2) was used in today's design question. Finally, they write one sentence connecting today's work back to the anchoring phenomenon: 'The Rift Valley pyramidal grain bin and the Kericho tea-leaf bucket are both frustums — their volumes differ because their base shapes differ, but the same formula structure governs both.'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your cumulative model — the diagram you have been building since Lesson 1. Today we add the pyramidal frustum panel. Draw it, label it, and write the formula. You have 6 minutes.' [Circulate and check that learners label A₁ and A₂ on the CORRECT faces — the two parallel faces — not the slant faces. Common error: labelling slant height as h. If observed, say: 'Remember — h is always perpendicular, straight down, between the two flat faces. Is your h pointing straight down?' WAIT 10 seconds.] After 6 minutes: 'Now write the structural link sentence and the arrow to Similarity and Enlargement. 3 minutes.' After 3 minutes: 'Finally, write your one sentence connecting today to the Kericho phenomenon. 2 minutes.' Close: 'Hold up your cumulative model. You now have five panels — cylinder, cone, conical frustum, pyramidal frustum, and the structural link. Three more lessons and you will use all of this to design your own container. Well done.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative annotated model building: requiring learners to physically add each lesson's content to a single growing diagram externalises the unit's conceptual progression. The cross-strand annotation arrow (to Similarity & Enlargement) makes mathematical coherence visible. The phenomenon-connection sentence ensures that every lesson phase closes the loop back to the anchoring context, sustaining the inquiry narrative across all eight lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators: (a) the pyramidal frustum panel shows A₁ and A₂ on the parallel faces (not slant faces) and h as perpendicular height; (b) the structural link sentence correctly uses the phrase 'geometric mean' or equivalent; (c) the phenomenon-connection sentence specifically names 'the Kericho tea-leaf bucket' or 'the Rift Valley grain bin' — generic sentences are flagged for revision. Teacher photographs 6–8 models (a purposive sample including strong and weak examples) for whole-class sharing at the start of Lesson 6.

LESSONS.teacherReflection:
After the lesson, reflect on the following questions and record brief notes in your professional journal:
1. PREDICTION QUALITY: Did learners' opening predictions reveal sound reasoning about base areas, or were most relying only on height? If learners compared base areas spontaneously, this suggests strong transfer from Sub-Strand 2.1 (Similarity and Enlargement) — note this for the Lesson 6 introduction.
2. FORMULA STRUCTURE: When learners colour-coded the two formulas side by side, did they articulate the 'geometric mean' idea independently, or did it require teacher prompting? If it required prompting, plan an additional 5-minute consolidation at the start of Lesson 6.
3. PART (d) — VOLUME SCALE FACTOR: Was the cross-strand connection to Similarity and Enlargement (k³ = 2 → k = ∛2) accessible to most groups, or did it cause significant difficulty? If more than one-third of groups could not start part (d), consider a brief whole-class worked example at the beginning of Lesson 6 before moving to pyramids with non-square bases.
4. DQB ENTRIES: Review the sticky notes or workbook entries. Are learners' 'new questions' converging on the culminating design challenge (choosing dimensions for a target capacity), or are there unexpected gaps (e.g., confusion about what 'perpendicular height' means in a frustum)? Adjust Lesson 6 accordingly.
5. MODEL BUILDING: Were the A₁/A₂ labelling errors (labelling slant faces instead of parallel faces) widespread? If yes, begin Lesson 6 with a 3-minute 'spot the error' activity using a photograph of an incorrectly labelled model.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners observed a side-by-side derivation comparing the volume formula for a pyramidal frustum, V = ⅓h(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)), with the conical frustum formula from Lesson 4, revealing that both share an identical mathematical structure — one-third times height times the sum of the top area, the bottom area, and their geometric mean. They also observed scale drawings of the Kericho tea-leaf bucket (conical frustum) and a Rift Valley grain-storage bin (pyramidal frustum) with the same height but different base shapes.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Learners determined that the volume of a frustum of a square or rectangular pyramid is given by V = ⅓h(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)), where A₁ and A₂ are the areas of the two parallel faces and h is the perpendicular height. They computed that a pyramidal grain-storage bin (top side 30 cm, bottom side 20 cm, height 40 cm) has a volume of approximately 25 333 cm³ ≈ 25.33 litres and can hold approximately 18.24 kg of dry maize (density 0.72 kg/litre). They also applied the volume scale factor k³ = 2 (from Sub-Strand 2.1) to determine that doubling the capacity while keeping the height fixed requires scaling each side length by ∛2 ≈ 1.26.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Learners explained that the Kericho tea farmers' metal bucket (conical frustum) and the Rift Valley pyramidal grain bin hold very different amounts of water even at the same height because their base areas — and therefore the values of A₁, A₂, and √(A₁A₂) — are fundamentally different: circular bases are governed by πr², while square bases are governed by s². The formula structure is the same, but the base-area calculation changes depending on the shape of the cross-section, which is why containers that look similar in height can hold dramatically different volumes. This advances the driving question: to design a container of exact capacity, a farmer must choose the base shape and dimensions carefully, not just the height.

LESSONS.title: Problem Solving with Real Containers: Apply & DQB Update

slo.purpose: Learners apply volume and capacity formulas for cones, cylinders, and frustums to solve authentic Kenyan-context word problems, justify formula choices, and consolidate understanding of why the Kericho tea farmers' containers hold such different volumes despite similar appearances.
slo.knowledge: Learners demonstrate knowledge of the volume formulas for cones (V = ⅓πr²h), cylinders (V = πr²h), frustums of cones (V = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²)), and frustums of pyramids; the relationship 1 litre = 1000 cm³; and how container shape — not just apparent size — determines capacity.
slo.skills: Learners apply volume and capacity formulas to multi-step word problems; select appropriate formulas given a described container shape; convert between cm³ and litres; verify reasonableness of answers against the anchoring phenomenon; and communicate mathematical reasoning to peers.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate that mathematical precision in calculating volume and capacity has direct practical value in everyday Kenyan life — from sizing water storage tanks in Turkana to designing cooking vessels for communal githeri — and show respect for peers' solution strategies by listening actively during group presentations.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is the knowledge of volume and capacity useful?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lessons 1–5, learners established the cylinder–cone volume relationship (3:1), derived the frustum formula by subtraction of cones, and measured the actual Kericho tea containers. Lesson 6 is the application and consolidation lesson: learners transfer all accumulated knowledge to three new real-world Kenyan problems (a Turkana water tank, a githeri pot, and a drum-filling count), present and defend their solutions, and update the Driving Question Board with mature, formula-backed explanations — bringing the unit close to a full answer to the driving question.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials are used. If physical containers and water are used for verification, place absorbent cloths on desks and ensure learners handle cylindrical drums carefully to avoid tipping. Learners with mobility considerations should be seated where group materials are easily accessible.

LESSONS.overview: Learners work in groups on a structured set of three Kenyan-context word problems that require them to select and apply volume/capacity formulas for cones, cylinders, and frustums. Problem 1 asks groups to size a conical water-storage tank for a homestead in Turkana; Problem 2 requires calculating the capacity of a frustum-shaped cooking pot needed to prepare githeri for 100 people at a community event in Kisumu; Problem 3 determines how many frustum-shaped cups (like the metal tea-collection buckets from Kericho) are needed to fill a cylindrical storage drum. Groups present solutions on the board, justify their formula choices by connecting back to the anchoring phenomenon, and the class updates the Driving Question Board with consolidated understanding. The lesson ends with a teacher-led synthesis that directly answers the driving question using evidence built across all six lessons.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner individually reads the three problem stems (displayed on the board / ARES screen) without any numbers filled in, and writes a one-sentence prediction for EACH problem: (a) Which formula will be needed? (b) Will the answer be larger or smaller than the Kericho cylindrical drum's capacity (established in Lesson 4 as approximately 18.5 litres)? Learners commit their predictions in their exercise books before groups are formed. This low-stakes individual commitment activates prior schema and creates personal investment in the group work that follows.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the three problem stems with blanks where numbers will appear. Say: 'Before I give you the full numbers, I want each of you — on your own, in silence — to predict which formula you will need for each container shape and whether the answer will be bigger or smaller than our Kericho drum. You have 3 minutes. Write your prediction now.' Set a visible timer. After 3 minutes, cold-call 3 learners (one per problem) using name sticks: 'Achieng, which formula do you predict for Problem 1, and why?' Apply 12-second WAIT TIME before accepting the answer. After each response, ask a second learner: 'Kamau, do you agree with Achieng's prediction? What is your reasoning?' Do NOT confirm or correct at this stage — say: 'Hold that prediction. Your group work will tell you whether you were right.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction with Formula Identification — By requiring learners to name the formula before seeing numbers, this strategy forces retrieval of the cone, cylinder, and frustum formulas from memory and connects them to shape descriptions. It surfaces any residual misconceptions (e.g., using the cone formula for a frustum) that the group work will then resolve.
framework.formativeAssessment: Circulate and scan exercise books during the 3-minute prediction window. Observable indicators of readiness: learner writes a recognisable formula (even partially, e.g., '⅓πr²h') next to each problem stem. Flag any learner who writes the same formula for all three shapes — seat them in a group with a strong peer who can model formula selection during Problem Set work.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4 receive the full Problem Set card. PROBLEM 1 (Cone — Turkana): A family in Turkana wants to build an underground conical water-storage tank. The tank must hold at least 500 litres of water. The available excavation depth (height) is 120 cm. What minimum base radius must the tank have? Give your answer to 1 decimal place. PROBLEM 2 (Frustum of cone — Githeri pot): A community kitchen in Kisumu is preparing githeri for 100 people. Each person needs 1.5 litres of githeri. The cooking pot is a frustum of a cone with a top (open) radius of 35 cm, a base radius of 20 cm, and a height of 50 cm. (a) Calculate the volume of the pot in litres. (b) How many full pots must be cooked to feed all 100 people? PROBLEM 3 (Frustum cup vs Cylinder drum — Kericho link): The metal tea-collection cup used in Kericho is a frustum of a cone: top radius 9 cm, base radius 6 cm, height 14 cm. The cylindrical storage drum at the collection centre has radius 30 cm and height 50 cm. How many full cups of tea leaves must be emptied into the drum to fill it completely? Groups work through each problem, showing all steps: (i) identify the shape and write the formula, (ii) substitute values, (iii) calculate, (iv) state the answer with units, (v) write one sentence connecting the answer back to the anchoring phenomenon.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute Problem Set cards. Say: 'You have 25 minutes. Every member must be able to explain any step — I will cold-call individuals, not just the group reporter. Show every substitution step; do not skip lines.' Set a visible 25-minute timer. Circulate in a deliberate loop — visit each group at least twice. At the 8-minute mark, if any group is stuck on Problem 1, prompt: 'You need at least 500 litres. Convert that to cm³ first. What is 1 litre in cm³?' (10-second WAIT TIME). At the 15-minute mark, prompt Problem 2 groups who are only computing volume without answering part (b): 'You have the pot volume. Now how many pots? What operation do you need?' For Problem 3, if groups forget to link back to the phenomenon, prompt: 'Your answer tells you how many cups fill the drum. Does this match what you predicted about the cylinder holding more than the cone? Explain.' In the final 2 minutes, instruct each group to choose a reporter AND a 'challenger' (a different person who must be ready to answer one question about the working).
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Structured Problem Decomposition — The five-step scaffold (identify shape → write formula → substitute → calculate → connect to phenomenon) is an explicit sensemaking routine. It prevents learners from pattern-matching numbers into a memorised formula without understanding and ensures every calculation is tethered to the physical reality of the Kericho containers. The 'connect to phenomenon' step in particular bridges procedural fluency and conceptual understanding.
framework.formativeAssessment: While circulating, look for three specific indicators: (1) Does the group correctly write V = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²) for Problems 2 and 3 — not V = πr²h? (2) Does the group correctly convert 500 litres → 500 000 cm³ in Problem 1? (3) Does the phenomenon-connection sentence go beyond 'the drum holds more' to reference the mathematical ratio? Groups not meeting indicator (1) need targeted intervention before presentations begin.

framework.learnerExperience: Three groups (one per problem) present their full solution at the board — the reporter writes the working while the challenger stands ready. The rest of the class acts as a 'peer review panel': they must write one agreement and one probing question in their exercise books before the Q&A opens. After each presentation, the teacher facilitates 3 minutes of structured peer questioning. Following all three presentations, the teacher leads a 5-minute whole-class synthesis comparing the three container capacities side by side and re-anchoring every result to the Kericho phenomenon.
framework.teacherMoves: Invite Group A to present Problem 1. After they write the solution, cold-call their challenger: 'Otieno, explain why you divided 500 000 by (⅓π × 120) and not by (π × 120²).' WAIT 12 seconds. Open the floor: 'Panel — who has a probing question for Group A?' Accept 2 questions maximum. Repeat for Groups B and C. For the synthesis, draw a three-column comparison table on the board: Container | Formula used | Capacity (litres). Populate it live with class answers. Ask: 'Looking at this table — does anyone see a pattern between which formula gives the largest capacity for similar dimensions?' Cold-call 2 learners. Then say: 'Now look back at your prediction from the start of the lesson. Turn to your neighbour and tell them in one sentence whether your prediction was correct and what you understand now that you did not understand before.' Allow 90 seconds of pair talk, then cold-call 3 pairs.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim–Evidence–Reasoning (CER) Oral Presentation — Each presenting group must articulate a claim (the answer), cite evidence (the substituted formula and calculated value), and provide reasoning (the connection to the anchoring phenomenon). The peer-review panel structure makes the audience cognitively active rather than passive, and the three-column synthesis table makes the comparative pattern visible — directly addressing the driving question about why similar-looking containers hold different amounts.
framework.formativeAssessment: During presentations, listen for: (1) Does the reporter use correct mathematical vocabulary — 'slant height', 'radius', 'frustum', 'capacity in litres'? (2) Does the challenger's explanation reveal understanding of formula derivation (e.g., 'the frustum formula comes from subtracting a small cone from a large cone')? (3) Do peer-panel questions probe conceptual understanding (e.g., 'Why did you use R and r, not just one radius?') rather than only arithmetic checks? Record names of learners who demonstrate depth of reasoning for extension tasks.

framework.learnerExperience: The class revisits the Driving Question Board that has been built across Lessons 1–5. Each learner receives two sticky notes: one GREEN ('I can now explain…') and one ORANGE ('I still wonder…'). Learners write their notes individually (2 minutes), then one representative from each group places their group's GREEN note under the relevant column on the DQB (Cone, Cylinder, Frustum, or General Pattern). The teacher reads aloud three selected GREEN notes and two ORANGE notes, and the class votes (thumbs up/sideways/down) on whether each GREEN note fully answers part of the driving question. ORANGE notes are stored for Lesson 7 (model making and measurement).
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute sticky notes. Say: 'Two minutes — write on GREEN: one thing you can now explain about the Kericho farmers' containers that you could not explain at the start of this unit. Write on ORANGE: one thing you still genuinely wonder about.' After 2 minutes, invite groups to place GREEN notes. Read aloud: 'This group writes — [read note]. Class, thumbs: does this fully answer part of our driving question, or is there still a gap?' For each ORANGE note, say: 'We will carry this question into Lesson 7. I want you to hold onto this curiosity.' Before closing the DQB segment, point to the driving question poster and say: 'Based on today's problems — the Turkana tank, the githeri pot, the Kericho cup and drum — can someone give me the most complete answer we have so far to our driving question? You have 15 seconds to think, then I will cold-call.' WAIT 15 seconds. Cold-call 2 learners.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: DQB Progressive Revision — The DQB is not a display but a living epistemic record. By physically moving notes and voting on the completeness of explanations, learners engage in metacognitive monitoring: they distinguish between procedural answers ('I can calculate the frustum volume') and conceptual answers ('I can explain why the frustum holds more than the cone because it retains the wide middle section that the cone discards'). This distinguishes surface-level from deep understanding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect GREEN and ORANGE notes at the end of the lesson. Review overnight for two indicators: (1) GREEN notes that reference only a formula (not an explanation) signal procedural-only understanding — these learners need conceptual prompting in Lesson 7. (2) ORANGE notes that raise design questions ('How do we choose the radii to get exactly 500 litres?') indicate readiness for extension work on the frustum design task in Lesson 8.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to their running 'Container Capacity Model' — a diagram started in Lesson 1 showing the three Kericho containers side by side. They now add a fourth annotated layer to their model: (a) Label each container with its formula. (b) Add a 'capacity bar' drawn to scale next to each container (1 cm = 10 litres), based on the actual values calculated or measured across the unit. (c) Write a two-sentence 'Model Update Statement' below the diagram explaining why the cylindrical drum holds exactly three times the conical cover, and where the frustum-shaped bucket sits between them mathematically. Learners share their updated model with a partner and identify one difference between their two models.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Open your Container Capacity Model from Lesson 1. You have 7 minutes to add the three annotations I have written on the board. This is your cumulative record of what you have learned — make it clear enough that a fellow learner who missed this unit could understand it.' Write the three annotation tasks on the board. Circulate and prompt: 'Your capacity bar for the drum should be three times as long as the bar for the cone — does yours show that? If not, recalculate and adjust.' At 6 minutes, say: 'Share with your partner. Find ONE thing your partner's model shows that yours does not.' After 1 minute of partner sharing, cold-call 2 pairs: 'Wanjiku, what did you learn from your partner's model?' WAIT 10 seconds. Close by pointing to the driving question: 'Your model now visually answers why those three Kericho containers look the same size but hold such different amounts. You built that understanding across six lessons — that is the power of mathematical reasoning.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Scaled Visual Modelling — Drawing the capacity bar to scale transforms an abstract numerical answer into a spatial, proportional representation. This directly mimics the 'same apparent size, different volume' puzzle of the anchoring phenomenon and makes the 3:1 cylinder-to-cone ratio perceptually obvious. The Model Update Statement requires learners to translate the visual back into language, reinforcing dual coding of the mathematical concept.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect models at the end of class (or photograph them). Check for three specific indicators: (1) All three formulas are correctly labelled. (2) The capacity bars are approximately in the ratio cone : frustum : cylinder = 1 : ~1.5–2.5 : 3 (exact ratio depends on frustum dimensions used). (3) The Model Update Statement uses mathematical vocabulary ('one-third', 'frustum lies between', 'same base and height') and references the Kericho phenomenon by name. Learners whose bars are all equal length have not transferred the 3:1 insight and need a brief one-on-one check at the start of Lesson 7.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following questions: (1) During Problem Set work, did all groups correctly identify the frustum formula for Problems 2 and 3 without prompting — or did most groups default to the cylinder formula? If more than two groups used the wrong formula, the formula-identification scaffold needs to be made more explicit in Lesson 7 (e.g., a 'shape identification checklist' card). (2) During presentations, did challengers demonstrate conceptual understanding of where the frustum formula comes from, or did they only reproduce the calculation steps? If challengers could not explain the derivation, plan a 5-minute 'formula origin' retrieval activity at the start of Lesson 7. (3) Were the ORANGE sticky notes largely procedural ('I still wonder how to calculate') or conceptual/design-oriented ('I still wonder how to choose dimensions to hit a target capacity')? The ratio of procedural to design-oriented ORANGE notes will tell you whether learners are ready for the open-ended design challenge in Lesson 8. (4) Did the 80-minute period allow genuine group discussion and full presentations, or were you rushed during the DQB and model-building phases? If time was tight, consider assigning the Model Update Statement as a written homework task so that the DQB update receives full class attention.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Three different containers used by Kericho tea farmers — a cone, a cylinder, and a frustum-shaped metal bucket — appear nearly the same size when placed side by side, yet when filled with water the cylinder holds three times as much as the cone, and the frustum holds an amount between the two.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: The volume of a cone is exactly one-third the volume of a cylinder with the same base radius and height (V = ⅓πr²h vs V = πr²h). A frustum of a cone has volume V = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²), which is always greater than the cone alone but less than the full cylinder. These formulas allow us to calculate and compare the exact capacity of any container — including sizing a Turkana water tank, a Kisumu githeri pot, or counting how many Kericho tea cups fill a storage drum.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: The three Kericho containers look similar because they share roughly the same height and opening diameter, but their shapes distribute that space very differently. The cylinder fills every cross-section from base to top with a full circle of area πr². The cone tapers to a point, so most cross-sections are much smaller — it uses only one-third of the cylinder's space. The frustum keeps a wide base and a wide top, so it retains far more of the middle volume than the cone does, placing its capacity between the cone and the cylinder. By applying the correct formula to each shape, we can predict, compare, and design containers to hold exactly the capacity we need.
