LESSONS.title: Project: Model Making & Measurement — Frustum, Pyramid Frustum, and Cone Containers

slo.purpose: Learners design and physically construct model containers shaped as a frustum of a cone, a frustum of a pyramid, and a cone using locally available materials (cardboard from cereal boxes, old packaging). They measure actual dimensions of their models, calculate theoretical volumes and capacities, then verify experimentally by filling with water or sand — connecting every measurement back to the Kericho tea farmers' three containers that anchor the whole unit.
slo.knowledge: Learners demonstrate knowledge of the volume formulas for a cone (V = ⅓πr²h), a frustum of a cone (V = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²)), and a frustum of a pyramid (V = ⅓h(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂))), and understand that 1 litre = 1000 cm³ for converting between volume and capacity.
slo.skills: Learners measure physical dimensions (radii/side lengths of top and bottom faces, slant height, perpendicular height) using a ruler or tape measure; calculate theoretical volumes and capacities using correct formulae; fill models with water or sand to obtain experimental capacity; compute percentage discrepancy between theoretical and experimental values; and document the process using photographs or short video clips.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the utility of mathematics in real-life design and manufacturing contexts (such as fabricating tea-collection containers for Kericho farmers); demonstrate persistence when experimental results do not match theory; and show respect for peers' contributions during group construction and discussion.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is the knowledge of volume and capacity useful?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Across the first six lessons learners unpacked why the cylindrical drum holds exactly three times the conical cover (V_cylinder = 3 × V_cone for equal base and height), derived the frustum formula by removing a smaller cone from a larger one, and applied all three formulae to real containers. In Lesson 7 learners now become the designers: they build their own scale-model versions of the three Kericho containers, take real measurements, compute theoretical capacities, and test them experimentally — transforming abstract formulae into tangible, testable objects and bringing the driving question one step from a full answer.
slo.safetyNotes: Scissors and craft knives must only be used under teacher supervision and always directed away from the body. Water used for filling models must be contained in a tray or basin to prevent slipping hazards on the floor. Learners with cuts or open wounds should wear gloves or assign measuring/recording roles instead of water-handling roles. All waste cardboard offcuts must be collected and placed in a bin — do not litter the classroom.

LESSONS.overview: Learners work in groups of four to construct three model containers from cardboard: (1) a cone, (2) a frustum of a cone, and (3) a frustum of a square pyramid. Each group uses cereal-box cardboard, a ruler, compass, protractor, scissors, and tape. After construction, they measure the relevant dimensions of each model, apply the appropriate volume formula to calculate theoretical capacity in millilitres/litres, then fill the model with water or fine dry sand measured in a graduated cylinder to obtain an experimental capacity. Groups record both values, compute the percentage discrepancy, and discuss possible sources of error. The lesson culminates in a gallery display of models and a whole-class discussion connecting measured discrepancies back to the phenomenon: just as real Kericho tea-collection containers have manufacturing tolerances, our models show that small errors in dimension produce measurable errors in capacity — reinforcing why precise measurement and correct formula choice matter.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group receives three pre-drawn net templates (cone, frustum of cone, frustum of square pyramid) on plain paper with blank dimension labels. Before cutting anything, learners predict — individually in their exercise books — which of the three finished models will have the greatest capacity, which the least, and by roughly how much. They also estimate the dimensions they will try to achieve (e.g., 'I think our cone will be about 10 cm tall and hold about 100 mL'). Predictions are written using the sentence frame: 'I predict the [shape] will hold the most because…'
framework.teacherMoves: Display the three blank net templates on the board. Say: 'Before we build anything, I want every one of you to be a scientist — make a prediction you can test. Look at these three nets. Which finished container do you think will hold the most water? Which will hold the least? Write your prediction AND your reason in your exercise book right now. You have 3 minutes — go.' [Allow 3 minutes of silent individual writing.] After 3 minutes: 'Turn to your neighbour and share your prediction in 30 seconds each.' [Allow 1 minute pair-share.] Cold-call 3 learners — choose one from a high-confidence hand-raiser, one from a non-volunteer, one from a different gender. Ask each: 'What did you predict, and what is your mathematical reason?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds after each question before prompting.] Record the three predictions on the board in a T-chart labelled 'Our Prediction' and 'Our Reason'. Say: 'We will return to these predictions at the end of the lesson. Keep them honest — do not change them once we start building.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Prediction Journaling with a Sentence Frame — activates prior knowledge of the three volume formulae from Lessons 3–6 and creates cognitive commitment that will be productively disrupted when experimental results arrive. Writing before sharing prevents groupthink and gives the teacher rapid formative data on which formulae learners can recall.
framework.formativeAssessment: Circulate during the 3-minute writing window and scan exercise books. Observable indicator of readiness: learner has written a specific numerical estimate (not just 'the cylinder holds more') and referenced at least one dimension or formula variable (e.g., 'because V = ⅓πr²h so a cone with the same base as the frustum will hold less'). If fewer than half the class can produce a formula reference, pause and do a 2-minute choral recall of the three formulae on the board before proceeding.

framework.learnerExperience: Groups construct their three cardboard models following the net templates. The cone net requires learners to calculate the slant length l = √(h² + r²) to draw the correct sector. The frustum-of-cone net requires two concentric circles (radii R and r for the base and top) plus the lateral curved band. The frustum-of-pyramid net requires four trapezoidal faces plus top and bottom squares. After cutting and taping, each group measures: (a) for cone — base radius r and perpendicular height h; (b) for frustum of cone — bottom radius R, top radius r, and perpendicular height h; (c) for frustum of pyramid — bottom side length a, top side length b, and perpendicular height h. All measurements are recorded in a group results table drawn in exercise books. Groups then fill each model with water (or dry sand) using a graduated cylinder/measuring cup and record the experimental volume in mL.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute materials (cardboard sheets, rulers, compasses, scissors, tape, basin of water, 250 mL graduated cylinders). Say: 'Each group will build all three models. Before you cut, the measurer in your group must write the target dimensions on the net in pencil — agree on them as a group. For the cone, decide: what height h and base radius r do you want? For the frustum of a cone, decide R, r, and h. For the pyramid frustum, decide a, b, and h. Write these target dimensions down before you cut anything.' [Allow 5 minutes for planning and marking dimensions.] Circulate — prompt groups who have not yet written target dimensions: 'Tell me your target R, r, and h for the frustum before you cut.' After models are built (approximately 25 minutes of construction): 'Now measure your ACTUAL dimensions — the model may not be exactly what you planned. Measure three times and take the average.' [WAIT TIME: allow 5 minutes for measurement.] When filling with water: 'Use the graduated cylinder. Fill slowly. Record to the nearest 5 mL. Do this twice and average the two readings.' Cold-call 2 groups mid-construction to share one challenge they have encountered: [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds] 'Group 3 — what is the hardest part of making the frustum of cone net? Why?' and 'Group 5 — how did you work out the slant height for your cone net?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Hands-On Model Construction with Targeted Measurement Recording — learners experience the physical reality that 'h' in the formula is the perpendicular (vertical) height, not the slant height, a distinction that is easy to overlook when working only on paper. Requiring measurement of the actual built model (which may differ from the target) makes the connection between real-world manufacturing tolerance and mathematical precision explicit and observable.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use an observation checklist with three checkpoints: (1) Group has written target dimensions before cutting — yes/no; (2) Group correctly identifies perpendicular height (not slant height) when prompted — yes/no; (3) Group records both experimental trial readings and computes an average — yes/no. If a group confuses slant height with perpendicular height during measurement, intervene immediately: 'Show me where the perpendicular height is on this frustum. Drop an imaginary plumb-line from the centre of the top face straight down — that distance is h. Measure that, not the slant side.'

framework.learnerExperience: Using their actual measured dimensions, each group calculates theoretical volume for all three models: V_cone = ⅓πr²h; V_frustum-cone = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²); V_frustum-pyramid = ⅓h(a² + b² + ab). They convert volumes from cm³ to mL (1 cm³ = 1 mL) and to litres. They then compute the percentage discrepancy: % discrepancy = |(theoretical − experimental)| / theoretical × 100%. Each group discusses and writes at least two reasons why their experimental capacity differed from theory (e.g., gaps/overlaps in cardboard seams, irregular base, parallax when reading the graduated cylinder, the cardboard itself displacing volume). Groups then connect this explicitly to the Kericho phenomenon: 'If a metalworker in Kericho makes a bucket that is 1 cm shorter than the design, how much capacity does the farmer lose?'
framework.teacherMoves: Project (or write on the board) the three formulae with units clearly labelled. Say: 'Now comes the mathematics. Use your ACTUAL measured dimensions — not your targets — to calculate the theoretical volume in cm³. Then convert to mL and to litres. Then compare with your experimental reading and work out the percentage discrepancy. Show every step.' [Allow 10 minutes for calculation.] Circulate and check formula substitution — specifically watch for learners squaring only one radius term in the frustum formula. If spotted, ask: 'Read the formula aloud. How many radius terms are there? Which ones did you square?' After calculations: facilitate a 5-minute whole-class share. Cold-call 4 groups — one per model type plus one additional: 'Group 2 — what percentage discrepancy did you get for your cone, and what do you think caused it?' [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds.] Write all groups' percentage discrepancies on the board in a class results table. Ask: 'Look at the discrepancies for the frustum of cone across all groups. Are they bigger or smaller than for the cone? Why might that be?' [WAIT TIME: 15 seconds, then take 2 hands.] Finally: 'Now think about the Kericho bucket. If Achieng' the metalworker makes the bucket 1 cm shorter — h decreases by 1 cm — use your formula to estimate how many fewer millilitres the farmer can carry. Calculate it.' [Allow 3 minutes.]
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Discrepancy Analysis with Phenomenon Re-connection — rather than treating experimental error as a failure, learners are guided to see it as a mathematical insight: the frustum formula is sensitive to small changes in R, r, and h simultaneously, which explains why the Kericho metal bucket's capacity is so different from the cone despite similar outer appearance. This is the 'Explain' of the POE cycle and directly advances the driving question.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect each group's written calculation page. Observable indicators: (1) Correct formula stated with all variables labelled; (2) Units consistently in cm and cm³ throughout before conversion; (3) Percentage discrepancy computed correctly using the formula; (4) At least two physically plausible sources of error identified. Flag any group whose theoretical volume is more than 40% away from the experimental — this almost always indicates that slant height was used instead of perpendicular height, and requires immediate individual re-teaching.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group writes one new sticky note (or index card) to add to the class Driving Question Board. The note must complete one of two sentence starters: (A) 'We can now explain… [part of the driving question]' — for something this lesson has answered; or (B) 'We still need to find out… [remaining gap]' — for something unresolved. Groups also vote on which sticky note from previous lessons (Lessons 1–6) can now be moved from the 'Questions' column to the 'Explained' column based on today's evidence. The teacher leads a 3-minute whole-class review of the DQB, noting what has been explained and what remains for Lesson 8.
framework.teacherMoves: Direct learners to the DQB display. Say: 'You have 4 minutes as a group to write your DQB card. Choose sentence starter A if you can now fully explain something about our Kericho farmers' containers. Choose starter B if today's lesson raised a new question you want answered.' [Allow 4 minutes.] Invite one representative from each group to place their card on the board and read it aloud in one sentence. [WAIT TIME: 10 seconds between each group.] Then say: 'Scan the old cards from Lessons 1 to 6. Raise your hand if you see a question card that today's project has fully answered — we can move it to the Explained column.' Cold-call 2 volunteers to nominate a card and explain why it can be moved. [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds per volunteer.] Summarise: 'Here is where we stand. We can now explain why the Kericho cone, bucket and drum hold different amounts — we have the formulae AND we have built and tested physical models. What remains for Lesson 8 is…' [preview the capstone lesson].
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative DQB Curation — making learners explicitly classify their new knowledge as 'explained' versus 'still open' builds metacognitive awareness and reinforces that the driving question is answered progressively, not all at once. Moving old question cards to the Explained column gives a visible, motivating record of intellectual progress across the unit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Read all new DQB cards after the lesson. Observable indicator of understanding: the 'We can now explain' card must reference a specific formula, a specific shape (cone/frustum), or the experimental verification process — not a vague statement like 'we know more about volume.' Cards that are vague are returned to the group at the start of Lesson 8 with the prompt: 'Add one formula or measurement to make this more specific.'

framework.learnerExperience: Groups arrange their three finished models on their desk as a mini-gallery, with a hand-written label card for each model showing: shape name, actual measured dimensions, theoretical volume (cm³ and litres), experimental volume (mL), and percentage discrepancy. Each group also produces a one-page 'Design Sheet' in their exercise book: a labelled diagram of each model with dimensions, the formula used, the full calculation, and a one-sentence reflection on the biggest source of error. At least one learner in each group photographs the three models together alongside the label cards using a phone or tablet. The teacher collects one photograph per group (or accepts a printed image) as the documentary evidence for the project assessment. The lesson closes with learners returning to their original predictions from Phase 1 and writing a two-sentence reflection: 'My prediction was [correct/partially correct/incorrect] because…'
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You have 8 minutes to write your label cards and complete your Design Sheet. The label card must show six things — I will write them on the board.' [Write: 1. Shape name. 2. Measured dimensions. 3. Theoretical volume in cm³. 4. Theoretical capacity in litres. 5. Experimental volume in mL. 6. % discrepancy.] Circulate and prompt any group that has left a label blank: 'You have a blank space for percentage discrepancy — finish that calculation before you display.' After 8 minutes: 'Take your photograph now. Make sure all three models and all three label cards are visible in the frame.' Conduct a 3-minute gallery walk — ask learners to silently look at two other groups' models and label cards. Then say: 'Back to your seats. Open your exercise book to your prediction from the very start of today's lesson. Write two sentences: was your prediction correct, and what does the mathematics tell you now?' Cold-call 2 learners to share their reflection aloud. [WAIT TIME: 12 seconds each.] Close by saying: 'The Kericho farmers' bucket looks similar to the cone and the drum, but today you proved with your own hands and your own calculations that the mathematics explains every difference in capacity. In Lesson 8 we will use everything we have built and proved to answer our driving question fully and present our solution.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Gallery Display with Prediction Revisit — anchoring the physical model display to the original written prediction closes the POE (Predict–Observe–Explain) cycle explicitly. The two-sentence reflection requires learners to reconcile their intuition with the mathematical evidence, consolidating the conceptual shift from 'shapes that look similar hold similar amounts' to 'volume depends precisely on the formula, and small dimensional changes produce measurable capacity differences.'
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect the Design Sheet (one per learner, drawn in exercise book). Observable indicators: (1) All three models have a correctly labelled diagram with at least three dimensions marked; (2) The correct formula is stated and correctly applied for each shape; (3) Percentage discrepancy is calculated and a physically plausible error source is named; (4) The prediction reflection is specific and references the formula or a measured dimension. Use this as the project formative rating against the KICD rubric descriptor: 'The learner accurately determines the volume and capacity of cones, frustum of a cone, and frustum of a pyramid.'

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect on the following: (1) Did all groups successfully identify perpendicular height as distinct from slant height during measurement? If not, this misunderstanding must be explicitly corrected at the start of Lesson 8 before any capstone calculations. (2) What was the typical percentage discrepancy across the class? A class median discrepancy above 20% suggests that cardboard construction introduced too much leakage/irregularity — for a future iteration, consider sealing model bases with masking tape or using plastic cups as the frustum base to reduce water loss. (3) Were the DQB 'We can now explain' cards specific enough to demonstrate formula-level understanding? If more than a third of the class produced vague cards, build a 5-minute DQB re-visit into the opening of Lesson 8. (4) Did the prediction-revisit reflection reveal lingering misconceptions — for example, learners who still attribute the difference in capacity to the 'opening size' rather than the full three-dimensional formula? These learners need a targeted follow-up question at the start of Lesson 8: 'If I keep the same top and bottom radius but double the height of the Kericho bucket, how does the volume change? Use the formula to show me.' (5) Consider which group's model set would make the strongest anchor display for Lesson 8's capstone — select the group with the most precise construction (lowest % discrepancy) AND the group with the highest discrepancy, so learners can compare and discuss why precision matters in real container design.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: Learners built three cardboard model containers (a cone, a frustum of a cone, and a frustum of a square pyramid), measured their actual dimensions, and filled them with water to determine experimental capacity — observing directly that the three shapes, even when built to similar heights and base widths, hold measurably different amounts of water, mirroring the Kericho farmers' containers.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: Learners applied V = ⅓πr²h for the cone, V = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²) for the frustum of a cone, and V = ⅓h(a² + b² + ab) for the frustum of a pyramid to compute theoretical capacity in cm³ and litres; they converted between cm³ and mL (1 cm³ = 1 mL); and they quantified the difference between theoretical and experimental capacity as a percentage discrepancy, identifying measurement and construction error as the cause.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: Learners can now explain that the Kericho tea farmers' cone, bucket (frustum of cone), and cylindrical drum hold such different amounts not because of how similar they look on the outside, but because their internal three-dimensional shapes obey fundamentally different volume formulae — and that even a 1 cm error in manufacturing a container's height or radius produces a calculable and significant change in the amount of tea it can carry.

slo.purpose: To consolidate all five specific learning outcomes for Sub-Strand 2.7 by presenting project models, completing the Driving Question Board, constructing a final annotated volume-relationship diagram, and demonstrating mastery through a written class activity.
slo.knowledge: Learners recall and integrate: (a) the formula for volume/capacity of a cone and pyramid; (b) the one-third relationship between a cone and its enclosing cylinder (and pyramid and its enclosing prism); (c) the frustum formula derived by subtraction of cones/pyramids; (d) unit conversions between cm³, litres and millilitres; (e) sources of measurement error in physical models.
slo.skills: Learners are able to: (a) determine the volume and capacity of cones and pyramids; (b) compute volume and capacity of a frustum of a cone; (c) calculate the volume and capacity of a frustum of a pyramid; (d) apply volume and capacity reasoning to design a container of specified capacity; (e) communicate mathematical reasoning through annotated diagrams and written explanations.
slo.attitudes: Learners appreciate the utility and aesthetic value of volume and capacity mathematics in everyday Kenyan life; demonstrate intellectual honesty when comparing predicted versus calculated values and explaining sources of error; show respect for peers' project work during gallery presentations.
slo.keyInquiry: Why is the knowledge of volume and capacity useful?
slo.purposeInStoryline: This is the culminating lesson of the unit. Learners have, across Lessons 1–7, built understanding of cylinder, cone, pyramid and frustum volumes. In Lesson 8 they bring everything together: groups present their frustum-container project models, compare calculated and measured capacities, and explain discrepancies. The whole class then constructs a final annotated diagram that captures the complete volume-relationship story — from the Kericho farmers' cylindrical drum, conical sisal cover and metal bucket (frustum) encountered in Lesson 1, to the full algebraic derivations. The DQB columns are completed. A written class activity formally assesses all five SLOs. Learners articulate what they now know versus what they predicted in Lesson 1, closing the anchoring phenomenon loop.
slo.safetyNotes: When handling physical containers filled with water during project demonstrations, ensure floor surfaces are kept dry to prevent slipping. Learners should place containers on a tray or basin. No sharp metallic edges on homemade models should be left exposed — tape or file all cut edges before the presentation session.

LESSONS.overview: Lesson 8 is the 80-minute culminating session for Sub-Strand 2.7. It opens with a brief Predict phase in which learners revisit their Lesson 1 predictions about the Kericho farmers' three containers and privately write what they now believe. Groups then present their frustum-container project models (Observe/Evidence phase) in a structured gallery walk, sharing both calculated capacities and physically measured volumes using water. In the Explain phase, the teacher facilitates whole-class construction of a final annotated diagram showing the volume relationships: V_cylinder = 3 × V_cone (same base and height); V_frustum = V_big_cone − V_small_cone; and the parallel relationships for pyramids and their frustums. The Driving Question Board is completed collaboratively, with learners moving evidence cards to the 'Answered' column and articulating remaining uncertainties. The lesson closes with a 25-minute written class activity assessing all five SLOs, followed by a 5-minute teacher-led debrief connecting every answer back to the Kericho phenomenon.

framework.learnerExperience: Each learner opens their exercise book to the prediction entry they made in Lesson 1 about the Kericho farmers' three containers. They silently re-read their original prediction, then write a 3-sentence 'revised prediction' in a different colour: (1) what they now believe about WHY the cylinder holds three times as much as the cone; (2) how much MORE the frustum bucket holds than the cone; and (3) what mathematical tool they would use to design a frustum that holds exactly 20 litres. Learners then share with their shoulder partner (Think-Pair) before two pairs are cold-called to share with the class.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the anchoring phenomenon photograph (or sketch on the board) of the three Kericho containers side by side — the cylindrical drum, the conical sisal cover, and the metal frustum bucket — labelled with their shared height (h = 30 cm) and shared opening diameter (d = 28 cm). Say verbatim: 'In Lesson 1 you made a prediction about these three containers. Before we present our projects, I want you to meet your Lesson 1 self. Open your books to that page.' Allow 3 minutes of silent individual writing. Then say: 'Share your revised prediction with your shoulder partner. You have 90 seconds.' After pair sharing, cold-call exactly 2 pairs using the class register (row 3, seat 2; row 5, seat 4). For each response, probe: 'What evidence from our lessons made you change your mind?' Apply 12-second WAIT TIME before accepting the answer. Record key phrases from responses on the board under the heading 'What we NOW believe' — this will anchor the DQB completion in Phase 4.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict–Revisit Strategy: By returning to their original Lesson 1 written prediction and comparing it against current understanding, learners engage in metacognitive reflection — a core sensemaking move. Seeing their own earlier misconceptions in writing makes conceptual change visible and personally meaningful, motivating the final explanation phase.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Each learner's revised prediction explicitly names the V = (1/3)πr²h relationship for the cone and references the frustum subtraction formula. Teacher circulates during the 3-minute writing window and scans for learners who still write vague answers (e.g., 'because the shapes are different') — these learners are flagged and will be specifically monitored during the written assessment in Phase 5.

framework.learnerExperience: Each of the 5–6 project groups displays their frustum-container model on their desk alongside: (a) a completed project data sheet showing the measured dimensions (R, r, h), their calculated volume in cm³ and capacity in litres, and the target capacity they were designing for; (b) a 250 ml graduated measuring cylinder or calibrated bottle used to physically measure the water volume their container actually holds. During a 12-minute structured gallery walk, learners rotate through every group's display in 2-minute slots, using a Gallery Observation Sheet to record: Group name | Target capacity (L) | Calculated capacity (L) | Measured capacity (L) | % error. In the final 8 minutes, each group stands by their model and delivers a 90-second verbal summary: 'Our container is a frustum of a cone / pyramid. We designed it to hold ___ litres. Our formula gave ___ litres. When we filled it with water it held ___ litres. The difference is because ___.'
framework.teacherMoves: Before the gallery walk begins, distribute the Gallery Observation Sheet and model how to calculate percentage error: write on the board '% error = |calculated − measured| ÷ calculated × 100%' and work through one fictional example: 'Group Simba calculated 18.4 L but measured 17.1 L. What is the % error? Work it out — you have 30 seconds.' Cold-call 1 learner. Confirm: '(18.4 − 17.1) ÷ 18.4 × 100% ≈ 7.1%.' During the gallery walk, circulate and pose to individual learners: 'Point to R and r on this model. Which one is bigger and why?' and 'If this group made R and r both larger by the same amount, would the volume increase, decrease or stay the same — explain.' Apply 12-second WAIT TIME at each probe. After the group verbal summaries, ask the whole class: 'Which group had the smallest percentage error? What did they do differently in construction?' Cold-call 3 learners for responses.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Evidence-to-Explanation Gallery Walk: Learners physically interact with multiple peer models, compute percentage error, and hear groups articulate their own sources of discrepancy. This data-rich observation phase provides concrete, multi-group evidence that the frustum formula is consistently predictive, while also surfacing the real-world gap between mathematical calculation and physical measurement — a key scientific and engineering practice (Planning and Carrying Out Investigations; Analysing and Interpreting Data).
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Each learner's completed Gallery Observation Sheet contains correct percentage error calculations for at least 4 groups. Groups' verbal summaries explicitly name a geometric source of error (e.g., 'the walls of our model were not perfectly straight so the top radius was slightly smaller than we measured') rather than a vague one (e.g., 'we made a mistake'). Teacher collects two randomly selected Gallery Observation Sheets from different rows to check calculation accuracy.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in their project groups to construct a Final Annotated Diagram in their exercise books. The diagram must show all four solids studied — cylinder, cone, square pyramid, frustum of cone — drawn to roughly the same height and base, each labelled with its volume formula. Arrows between shapes must be annotated with the mathematical relationship: a double-headed arrow between cylinder and cone labelled 'V_cylinder = 3 × V_cone (same base, same height)'; an arrow from frustum to big cone and small cone labelled 'V_frustum = V_big − V_small = (1/3)πh(R² + Rr + r²)'. At the bottom of the diagram, learners write one sentence connecting each shape back to the Kericho phenomenon: e.g., 'The cylindrical drum holds 3 × the conical sisal cover because they share the same base diameter and height.' Groups then share their diagram with an adjacent group and give one piece of written feedback on a sticky note.
framework.teacherMoves: Begin by drawing the outline of the four shapes on the board — large enough for learners to see the proportional size differences. Say verbatim: 'I am going to draw the skeleton. Your job is to fill in every formula, every relationship arrow, and every connection to the Kericho containers. You have 10 minutes in your groups.' Set a visible timer. After 10 minutes, cold-call one group to come to the board and annotate the class diagram, narrating each step aloud. After they annotate the cone–cylinder relationship, ask: 'Can someone from a different group give me the frustum formula and explain where it comes from — in one sentence?' Apply 12-second WAIT TIME. Cold-call 2 learners. Then ask: 'What is the capacity in litres of a cone with the same dimensions as the Kericho cylindrical drum — radius 14 cm, height 30 cm?' Allow 90 seconds of individual working. Cold-call 1 learner: expected answer V_cone = (1/3) × π × 14² × 30 ≈ 6,158 cm³ ≈ 6.16 L. Confirm and say: 'Now you understand why the conical sisal cover holds only about 6 litres while the cylindrical drum holds about 18.5 litres — and the frustum bucket sits between them depending on its r.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Annotated Diagram Synthesis (Science and Engineering Practice: Developing and Using Models): Constructing a diagram that simultaneously displays all four formulae and their inter-relationships forces learners to organise knowledge into a coherent relational structure — moving from isolated procedural knowledge (calculating one volume at a time) to integrated conceptual understanding (how all the shapes relate through the one-third ratio and the subtraction principle). Connecting each arrow back to the Kericho phenomenon ensures the model is anchored in evidence rather than being purely abstract.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Learner diagrams contain (a) all four correct volume formulae with no algebraic errors; (b) the annotated V_cylinder = 3 × V_cone arrow; (c) the frustum = big cone − small cone derivation arrow; (d) at least one Kericho-phenomenon sentence per shape. Teacher checks 4–5 books during group work. Groups that omit the pyramid frustum formula are prompted: 'How is the frustum of a pyramid different from the frustum of a cone? Write the formula and add the arrow.'

framework.learnerExperience: The class DQB (displayed on the wall or front board since Lesson 1) has three columns: 'What we wonder', 'Evidence we have gathered', 'What we now know/can explain'. Learners spend 3 minutes in pairs reviewing all cards in the 'What we wonder' column and deciding which questions have now been fully answered. A class representative physically moves answered cards to the 'What we now know' column and writes a one-line answer on the card. Any question that remains unanswered or only partially answered is moved to a new column: 'Questions for further study'. The final 2 minutes involve each learner writing in their book: 'In Lesson 1 I predicted ___. I now know ___ because ___.'
framework.teacherMoves: Stand at the DQB and read aloud the original Driving Question: 'Why do the tea farmers' containers — a cone, a cylinder and a bucket — look nearly the same size but hold such different amounts of water, and how can we use mathematics to design a frustum-shaped container that holds exactly the capacity we need?' Then say verbatim: 'This was our question for eight lessons. Look at this board. In pairs, decide — have we answered it? Give me a thumbs up when your pair agrees.' Wait until at least 80% show thumbs up (approximately 10 seconds). Ask one pair: 'State the complete answer in two sentences.' After the class representative moves cards, teacher reads aloud the final answer card for the main driving question. Ask: 'Is there anything on this board we could NOT fully answer? What further mathematics would we need?' Accept 2 responses. This surfaces intellectual humility and models scientific practice of identifying the boundaries of current knowledge.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board Completion (Science and Engineering Practice: Constructing Explanations): The DQB is a public, cumulative knowledge-tracking tool. Physically moving cards from 'wonder' to 'know' makes the arc of learning tangible and celebratory, while identifying residual questions models authentic scientific inquiry — real understanding always generates new questions. Comparing Lesson 1 predictions with final answers makes conceptual growth explicit.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicator: Each learner's written 'In Lesson 1 I predicted ___ / I now know ___' entry explicitly references at least one formula or mathematical relationship (not just a general statement). Teacher scans 6–8 books during the 2-minute writing window. Entries that remain at the level of 'I now know the shapes are different' are flagged as needing support during the written assessment.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners individually complete a structured written class activity (20 minutes) comprising five questions, one per SLO, all set in the Kericho tea-farming context. Q1 (SLO a — cone/pyramid): A conical sisal cover used by a Kericho farmer has a base diameter of 56 cm and a vertical height of 30 cm. Calculate its volume in cm³ and capacity in litres. Q2 (SLO b — frustum of cone): The metal bucket (frustum of cone) has a large base radius R = 14 cm, small base radius r = 9 cm and height h = 30 cm. Use the formula V = (1/3)πh(R² + Rr + r²) to calculate its volume in cm³ and capacity in litres. Q3 (SLO c — frustum of pyramid): A square frustum used as a tea-drying tray has a large base of side 20 cm, a small base of side 12 cm and height 15 cm. Calculate its volume. Q4 (SLO d — application/design): A farmer in Kericho needs a frustum-of-cone container that holds exactly 10 litres (10,000 cm³). She fixes h = 25 cm and r = 6 cm. Use the frustum formula to find R, correct to 1 decimal place. Q5 (SLO e — appreciation/explanation): In 3–4 sentences, explain why the cylindrical drum, conical cover and frustum bucket all have the same opening diameter and height yet hold different amounts. Use the formulae to support your answer. After 20 minutes, teacher leads a 5-minute oral debrief: cold-calls learners for each answer and connects every answer back to the Kericho phenomenon.
framework.teacherMoves: Distribute the written activity sheet face-down. Say verbatim: 'This activity covers everything we have learned in Sub-Strand 2.7. Every question is set in Kericho — these are real containers used by real farmers. Show all working. You have 20 minutes starting now.' Set timer visibly. Circulate quietly for the first 5 minutes — do not answer questions; instead, if a learner is stuck, point silently to the formula sheet displayed on the board (all four formulae written: V_cone = (1/3)πr²h; V_pyramid = (1/3)Ah; V_frustum_cone = (1/3)πh(R²+Rr+r²); V_frustum_pyramid = (h/3)(A₁+A₂+√(A₁A₂))). At the 15-minute mark, give a 5-minute warning. After collection, debrief Q1 by cold-calling 1 learner (expected: V = (1/3)×π×28²×30 ≈ 24,630 cm³ ≈ 24.63 L — note: diameter 56 cm means r = 28 cm, not 14 cm, so cone is much larger; confirm with class). Debrief Q2: cold-call 1 learner (expected: V = (1/3)×π×30×(196+126+81) = (1/3)×π×30×403 ≈ 12,662 cm³ ≈ 12.66 L). For Q5, cold-call 1 learner and require them to read their answer aloud; prompt: 'Which word in your answer shows you understand the ONE-THIRD relationship?' Close by saying: 'These are the containers of the Kericho tea farmers. You can now calculate exactly how much water — or tea — any of them holds. That is why the knowledge of volume and capacity is useful.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Authentic Assessment as Final Sensemaking (Science and Engineering Practice: Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking): The five-question written activity is not merely summative — it is the final sensemaking act of the unit. By requiring learners to apply every SLO within the single coherent context of the Kericho phenomenon, the assessment reinforces that the formulae are tools for explaining a real situation, not isolated procedures. The oral debrief after the written activity closes the explanation loop publicly, making each answer a shared class conclusion rather than a private grade.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observable indicators during debrief: (a) Q1 — learner correctly halves the diameter to get r = 28 cm before substituting; (b) Q2 — learner correctly expands R² + Rr + r² = 196 + 126 + 81 = 403; (c) Q3 — learner uses the pyramid frustum formula with A₁ = 400 cm², A₂ = 144 cm², √(A₁A₂) = 240 cm², giving V = (15/3)(400 + 144 + 240) = 5 × 784 = 3,920 cm³; (d) Q4 — learner sets up 10,000 = (1/3)π×25×(R²+6R+36) and solves to get R ≈ 11.4 cm; (e) Q5 — answer explicitly states V_cylinder = πr²h and V_cone = (1/3)πr²h so V_cylinder = 3 × V_cone, and places frustum between them because its formula accumulates area between R and r. Teacher marks written activities before the next lesson and returns with written feedback aligned to the KICD four-level rubric (Below Expectations / Approaches Expectations / Meets Expectations / Exceeds Expectations) for SLO indicators in Sub-Strand 2.7.

After the lesson, reflect on the following questions and record your responses in your professional journal:

1. PHENOMENON CLOSURE: Did learners articulate a complete, formula-supported explanation of why the three Kericho containers hold different volumes, or did some still rely on shape descriptions alone? What follow-up is needed?

2. PROJECT QUALITY: What was the average percentage error between calculated and measured capacities across the project groups? Groups with errors above 15% — what construction or measurement issues caused this? How would you adjust the project brief for the next cohort?

3. DQB COMPLETION: Were there any 'What we wonder' cards that could NOT be moved to 'What we now know'? If so, which sub-strand or future grade topic addresses them? Note these for the next unit introduction.

4. WRITTEN ASSESSMENT: After marking Q4 (the design/reverse-engineering question), what proportion of learners successfully rearranged the frustum formula to solve for R? If fewer than 60% succeeded, this algebraic manipulation skill requires reinforcement in strand 1.3 (Quadratic Equations) — note the cross-strand connection for the mathematics department meeting.

5. DIFFERENTIATION: Which learners consistently produced work at the 'Exceeds Expectations' level across phases 2–5? How will you extend them (e.g., challenge: derive the frustum formula from first principles by subtracting a small cone from a large cone algebraically)? Which learners were flagged during Phase 1 as still holding misconceptions — what targeted support will you provide?

The frustum keeps a wide bottom (radius R) and narrows only to a smaller circle (radius r, not zero), so it captures more volume than the cone but less than the cylinder. A Kericho farmer who needs a container of exactly 10 litres can use V = (1/3)πh(R² + Rr + r²), fix h and r to match available sheet-metal sizes, and solve for R — turning mathematics into a practical design tool.

FINAL_EXPLANATION.subjectLabel: Essential Mathematics Grade 10: Sub-strand 2.7 Volume and Capacity — Final Explanation
FINAL_EXPLANATION.instructions: This is your Final Explanation for the unit. Use what you have learned in all eight lessons about the Kericho tea farmers' three containers: the cylindrical drum (A), the conical sisal cover (B) and the metal frustum bucket (C). Write your answers in the space under each prompt. Use full sentences, show every step of any calculation, include units, and refer to the measurements from the lessons where a question asks you to. Use the formulas and ideas we developed in class, and explain why each one works as well as what it is.

sections.title: Part 1: The three containers and the 3 : 1 pattern
sections.prompt: In Lesson 1 the three Kericho containers were filled to the brim. The drum (A) held about 9.4 L, the conical cover (B) about 3.1 L and the metal bucket (C) about 6.5 L, even though all three have roughly the same height and opening diameter. (a) Work out the ratio of the capacity of A to the capacity of B and say what it suggests. (b) Describe the pouring experiment from Lesson 2 that showed this ratio, and say what you saw. (c) Starting from V = πr²h for the cylinder, show how you get the volume formula for the cone. (d) Explain in your own words why the cone holds less than the cylinder even though they have the same height and opening width.
sections.exemplar: (a) 9.4 ÷ 3.1 ≈ 3.03, so the ratio is about 3 : 1. The cylindrical drum holds about three times as much as the conical cover. (b) We filled a transparent cone with water and poured it into a matching cylinder with the same base radius r and the same height h. The cylinder was exactly full after the third pour, so V(cylinder) = 3 × V(cone). (c) Since V(cylinder) = 3 × V(cone), V(cone) = ⅓ × V(cylinder) = ⅓πr²h. (d) The cylinder keeps the same full circle of area πr² at every level from base to top. The cone narrows steadily to a point, so most of its cross-sections are much smaller circles. It therefore fills only one-third of the space the cylinder fills, even though it has the same height and opening width.

sections.title: Part 2: Where does the metal bucket fit?
sections.prompt: Container C, the metal bucket, is a frustum of a cone. (a) Where does its capacity (about 6.5 L) sit compared with the cone (about 3.1 L) and the cylinder (about 9.4 L)? (b) Explain how a frustum is related to two cones. (c) Write the volume formula for a frustum of a cone, where R is the top radius, r is the bottom radius and h is the vertical height, and state which two cone volumes are subtracted to obtain it. (d) Explain why the bucket holds more water than the cone even though both have the same height and top opening.
sections.exemplar: (a) The bucket's 6.5 L is more than the cone's 3.1 L but less than the cylinder's 9.4 L, so it sits between them. (b) A frustum is a large cone with a smaller cone cut off at the narrow end. The remaining piece is the frustum. (c) V(frustum) = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²). It comes from V(large cone) − V(small cone). We used similar triangles to eliminate the unknown full height of the large cone, and expanding the subtraction gives the three terms R², Rr and r². (d) Cutting off the narrow tip of the cone removes very little volume, because the tip is so thin. The frustum keeps a wide top (the opening) and only narrows to a smaller circle at the bottom, so it keeps much more of the middle volume than a cone that narrows to a point. It therefore holds more than the cone, but because it still narrows from top to bottom it cannot hold as much as the cylinder, which stays full-width all the way.

sections.title: Part 3: Pyramids, frustums of pyramids and units
sections.prompt: (a) In Lesson 3 you filled a square-based pyramid with rice and poured it into a cuboid with the same base and height. State what you found and write the volume formula for the pyramid. (b) Explain what the cone–cylinder result and the pyramid–cuboid result have in common. (c) Write the volume formula for a frustum of a square pyramid in terms of the areas A₁ and A₂ of its two parallel faces and the height h, and explain what is the same and what is different between this and the frustum of a cone. (d) A container has a volume of 9 400 cm³. Convert this to litres, and give the conversion relationships you used.
sections.exemplar: (a) It took 3 full pyramids to fill the cuboid, so V(pyramid) = ⅓ × base area × height. (b) In both cases the pointed solid (the cone or the pyramid) holds exactly one-third of the solid with the same base and height that surrounds it (the cylinder or the cuboid). This is true whether the base is circular or square. (c) V = ⅓h(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)). The structure is the same as for the frustum of a cone: one-third times the height times the sum of the two end areas and their geometric mean. What differs is how the areas are calculated: for a cone frustum A = πr², and for a square pyramid frustum A = s². (d) 1 cm³ = 1 mL and 1 000 cm³ = 1 L (also 1 m³ = 1 000 L). So 9 400 cm³ = 9 400 mL = 9.4 L.

sections.title: Part 4: Designing a container of exact capacity
sections.prompt: A Kericho farmer wants a new frustum-shaped metal bucket that holds 10 litres. Available sheet metal fixes the vertical height at h = 30 cm and the bottom radius at r = 8 cm. (a) Convert the target capacity to cm³. (b) Substitute into the frustum formula and write an equation for the top radius R. (c) Solve for R, giving your answer to 1 decimal place, and say whether it is a sensible size for a bucket with r = 8 cm. (d) If you built a model bucket like this and found that it held slightly more or less than 10 L when filled with water, give two possible reasons for the difference, based on your project in Lesson 7.
sections.exemplar: (a) 10 L = 10 × 1 000 cm³ = 10 000 cm³. (b) 10 000 = ⅓ × π × 30 × (R² + 8R + 64), which simplifies to 10 000 = 10π(R² + 8R + 64). Then R² + 8R + 64 = 1 000 ÷ π ≈ 318.3, so R² + 8R − 254.3 = 0. (c) Using the quadratic formula, R = (−8 + √(64 + 1017.2)) ÷ 2 = (−8 + 32.88) ÷ 2 ≈ 12.4 cm. Check: 12.4² + 8 × 12.4 + 64 = 153.76 + 99.2 + 64 = 316.96, and 10π × 316.96 ≈ 9 957 cm³ ≈ 10 L. A top radius of 12.4 cm (diameter about 25 cm) is wider than the bottom radius of 8 cm, so the bucket opens upwards like the Kericho bucket, and this is a sensible size. (d) Possible reasons: small errors in measuring the height or radii (even 1 cm makes a calculable change in capacity); the cut and folded cardboard or metal not forming a perfect shape; water not filled exactly to the brim or some left behind when poured. These explain the percentage discrepancy between theoretical and experimental capacity.

sections.title: Part 5: Answering the driving question
sections.prompt: Our driving question was: Why do the tea farmers' containers, a cone, a cylinder and a bucket, look nearly the same size but hold such different amounts of water, and how can we use mathematics to design a frustum-shaped container that holds exactly the capacity we need? Write a clear explanation of 6 to 8 sentences. Include (i) the relationship between the cylindrical drum and the conical cover, (ii) why the frustum bucket falls between them, (iii) how the formulas let a farmer design a container, and (iv) your answer to the KICD question: why is the knowledge of volume and capacity useful?
sections.exemplar: The drum, the conical cover and the bucket look the same size because they have roughly the same height and opening diameter, but their insides are shaped differently, so the area of each cross-section builds up differently from base to top. The cylinder keeps a full circle of area πr² at every level, so it holds the most. The cone narrows steadily to a point, so it holds exactly one-third of the matching cylinder, V = ⅓πr²h, which matches 3.1 L compared with 9.4 L. The frustum bucket is a large cone with a small cone removed, V = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²). It keeps a wide top opening and narrows only to a smaller circle at the bottom, not to a point, so it holds more than the cone but less than the cylinder (about 6.5 L). The same idea works for pyramids and their frustums, using V = ⅓h(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)). A farmer who wants a container of exactly 10 L can fix the height and one radius, then solve the formula for the other radius. Knowing volume and capacity is useful because it lets us compare, predict and design containers such as tanks, cooking pots, grain bins and tea buckets, saving materials and money and avoiding guesswork.

SUMMARY_TABLE.drivingQuestion: DRIVING QUESTION: Why do the tea farmers' containers — a cone, a cylinder and a bucket — look nearly the same size but hold such different amounts of water, and how can we use mathematics to design a frustum-shaped container that holds exactly the capacity we need?

lessons.title: The Kericho Container Puzzle: Anchoring the Phenomenon & Launching the Driving Question
lessons.observed: Three containers used by Kericho tea farmers — a cylindrical drum (A), a conical sisal cover (B), and a metal frustum bucket (C) — all with roughly the same height and opening diameter, were shown filled to the brim. Container A held ≈ 9.4 L, Container B held ≈ 3.1 L, and Container C held ≈ 6.5 L. The cylinder held almost exactly three times as much as the cone.
lessons.learned: Volume is measured in cm³ or m³; capacity is measured in mL or L. The conversion relationships are: 1 cm³ = 1 mL, 1 000 cm³ = 1 L, and 1 m³ = 1 000 L. The ratio of the cylinder's capacity to the cone's capacity (same height, same base) is 3 : 1 — a fact that is not yet explained but will be investigated across this unit.
lessons.explained: We cannot yet fully explain why containers of nearly the same height and opening diameter hold such different amounts. Our current best explanation is that the cone narrows to a point, leaving less interior space, while the cylinder stays the same width all the way down. We have posted our questions on the Driving Question Board and will build toward a complete mathematical explanation in the lessons ahead.

lessons.title: Cone vs. Cylinder — Deriving the Cone Volume Formula
lessons.observed: Learners filled a cone with water and poured it into a matching cylinder three times, directly observing that the cylinder was exactly full after the third pour — demonstrating V(cylinder) = 3 × V(cone) using containers that represent the Kericho tea-farmer drum and conical sisal cover.
lessons.learned: Learners derived the cone volume formula V = ⅓πr²h algebraically from the observed 1:3 ratio, calculated the capacity of the Kericho conical cover (r = 21 cm, h = 42 cm) as approximately 19 373 cm³ ≈ 19.4 litres, and confirmed it holds exactly one-third the volume of the matching cylindrical drum.
lessons.explained: Learners explained in writing why the conical sisal cover holds far less water than the cylindrical drum despite identical height and opening width, and updated their cumulative container diagram with the formula, the calculated capacity, and a ×3 ratio arrow — leaving a deliberate question mark on the metal bucket (frustum) as the next mathematical puzzle to solve.

lessons.title: Volume of Pyramids: Unlocking the One-Third Relationship
lessons.observed: Learners filled a card-stock square-based pyramid with rice and poured it into an identical-base-and-height cuboid, repeating until the cuboid was full. They recorded that it took 3 full pyramids to fill 1 cuboid, and used a ruler to measure the base and height of their pyramid model.
lessons.learned: V(pyramid) = ⅓ × base area × height; the same one-third relationship that links a cone to its cylinder also links a square-based pyramid to its cuboid. Learners also practised converting pyramid volumes from cm³ and m³ into litres (1 m³ = 1 000 litres) using grain-store problems from Eldoret, Kisumu, and the Rift Valley.
lessons.explained: The one-third factor in both V(cone) = ⅓ × πr² × h and V(pyramid) = ⅓ × b² × h reflects a geometric pattern: any pointed solid (apex tapering to a point) holds exactly one-third of its surrounding box, regardless of whether the base is circular or square. This explains why the pyramidal grain stores used by Kenyan farmers hold far less grain than a similarly sized cuboid store — and raises the question of how to compute the volume of the frustum-shaped metal bucket, which lies between these two extremes.

lessons.title: Introducing Frustums of Cones: Deriving the Volume Formula and Solving the Bucket Mystery
lessons.observed: Learners physically measured a frustum-shaped metal bucket (top radius R, bottom radius r, vertical height h) and observed a cone model placed alongside it, noticing that the frustum is a large cone with a small cone removed from the bottom.
lessons.learned: Learners derived V(frustum of cone) = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²) by subtracting V(small cone) from V(large cone), using similar-triangle reasoning to eliminate the unknown full height H. They calculated the Kericho bucket's capacity in litres and placed it correctly between the cone (~6.16 L) and the cylinder (~18.47 L), resolving the anchoring phenomenon.
lessons.explained: The frustum bucket holds more water than the cone because removing the narrow tip of the cone discards very little volume — the tip contributes almost nothing — while retaining the wide bottom section. The three terms R², Rr, r² in the formula arise algebraically from expanding the subtraction of two cone volumes and reflect the interplay between the large radius, the small radius, and their geometric mean. This is why containers of the same height and top diameter can hold dramatically different amounts depending on their shape.

lessons.title: Volume of Frustums of Pyramids — Designing the Perfect Grain-Storage Bin
lessons.observed: Learners observed a side-by-side derivation comparing the volume formula for a pyramidal frustum, V = ⅓h(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)), with the conical frustum formula from Lesson 4, revealing that both share an identical mathematical structure — one-third times height times the sum of the top area, the bottom area, and their geometric mean. They also observed scale drawings of the Kericho tea-leaf bucket (conical frustum) and a Rift Valley grain-storage bin (pyramidal frustum) with the same height but different base shapes.
lessons.learned: Learners determined that the volume of a frustum of a square or rectangular pyramid is given by V = ⅓h(A₁ + A₂ + √(A₁A₂)), where A₁ and A₂ are the areas of the two parallel faces and h is the perpendicular height. They computed that a pyramidal grain-storage bin (top side 30 cm, bottom side 20 cm, height 40 cm) has a volume of approximately 25 333 cm³ ≈ 25.33 litres and can hold approximately 18.24 kg of dry maize (density 0.72 kg/litre). They also applied the volume scale factor k³ = 2 (from Sub-Strand 2.1) to determine that doubling the capacity while keeping the height fixed requires scaling each side length by ∛2 ≈ 1.26.
lessons.explained: Learners explained that the Kericho tea farmers' metal bucket (conical frustum) and the Rift Valley pyramidal grain bin hold very different amounts of water even at the same height because their base areas — and therefore the values of A₁, A₂, and √(A₁A₂) — are fundamentally different: circular bases are governed by πr², while square bases are governed by s². The formula structure is the same, but the base-area calculation changes depending on the shape of the cross-section, which is why containers that look similar in height can hold dramatically different volumes. This advances the driving question: to design a container of exact capacity, a farmer must choose the base shape and dimensions carefully, not just the height.

lessons.title: Problem Solving with Real Containers: Apply & DQB Update
lessons.observed: Three different containers used by Kericho tea farmers — a cone, a cylinder, and a frustum-shaped metal bucket — appear nearly the same size when placed side by side, yet when filled with water the cylinder holds three times as much as the cone, and the frustum holds an amount between the two.
lessons.learned: The volume of a cone is exactly one-third the volume of a cylinder with the same base radius and height (V = ⅓πr²h vs V = πr²h). A frustum of a cone has volume V = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²), which is always greater than the cone alone but less than the full cylinder. These formulas allow us to calculate and compare the exact capacity of any container — including sizing a Turkana water tank, a Kisumu githeri pot, or counting how many Kericho tea cups fill a storage drum.
lessons.explained: The three Kericho containers look similar because they share roughly the same height and opening diameter, but their shapes distribute that space very differently. The cylinder fills every cross-section from base to top with a full circle of area πr². The cone tapers to a point, so most cross-sections are much smaller — it uses only one-third of the cylinder's space. The frustum keeps a wide base and a wide top, so it retains far more of the middle volume than the cone does, placing its capacity between the cone and the cylinder. By applying the correct formula to each shape, we can predict, compare, and design containers to hold exactly the capacity we need.

lessons.title: Project: Model Making & Measurement — Frustum, Pyramid Frustum, and Cone Containers
lessons.observed: Learners built three cardboard model containers (a cone, a frustum of a cone, and a frustum of a square pyramid), measured their actual dimensions, and filled them with water to determine experimental capacity — observing directly that the three shapes, even when built to similar heights and base widths, hold measurably different amounts of water, mirroring the Kericho farmers' containers.
lessons.learned: Learners applied V = ⅓πr²h for the cone, V = ⅓πh(R² + Rr + r²) for the frustum of a cone, and V = ⅓h(a² + b² + ab) for the frustum of a pyramid to compute theoretical capacity in cm³ and litres; they converted between cm³ and mL (1 cm³ = 1 mL); and they quantified the difference between theoretical and experimental capacity as a percentage discrepancy, identifying measurement and construction error as the cause.
lessons.explained: Learners can now explain that the Kericho tea farmers' cone, bucket (frustum of cone), and cylindrical drum hold such different amounts not because of how similar they look on the outside, but because their internal three-dimensional shapes obey fundamentally different volume formulae — and that even a 1 cm error in manufacturing a container's height or radius produces a calculable and significant change in the amount of tea it can carry.

lessons.explained: We can now fully explain the anchoring phenomenon: the cylindrical drum, the conical sisal cover and the metal frustum bucket look the same size because they share the same height and opening diameter, but their internal geometries — how cross-sectional area accumulates from base to top — differ fundamentally. The cylinder maintains a constant circular cross-section all the way up, so it accumulates the maximum possible volume. The cone tapers linearly to a point, cutting its volume to exactly one-third. The frustum keeps a wide bottom (radius R) and narrows only to a smaller circle (radius r, not zero), so it captures more volume than the cone but less than the cylinder. A Kericho farmer who needs a container of exactly 10 litres can use V = (1/3)πh(R² + Rr + r²), fix h and r to match available sheet-metal sizes, and solve for R — turning mathematics into a practical design tool.
